On 22 February 1452 the king and Douglas dined at Stirling. James asked him to dissolve the alliance, Douglas refused, and James stabbed him twice before his attendants joined in. The killing of a man under royal protection damaged James's standing.

The new earl, James, 9th Earl of Douglas, burned Stirling in March 1452. A parliament cleared the king of the murder. In August 1455 parliament disinherited the Douglases for treason, and James distributed their lands, creating new earldoms after 1457. He attacked English Berwick in 1455, exploiting the Wars of the Roses, and renounced the truce with England in May 1456.

James was killed at Roxburgh on 3 August 1460 when a bombard near him exploded, probably during a salute for the queen's arrival at the siege. The historian John Major blamed him for being over-curious in the matter of engines of war. The castle fell on 8 August, and James III was crowned at Kelso Abbey on 10 August. James II was buried at Holyrood Abbey. His widow Mary of Guelders became the leading figure in Scottish politics and was formally appointed regent in 1461. James has been described as a largely successful king who strengthened the Scottish monarchy.
james-iii-of-scotland: James was the first surviving son of King James II and Mary of Guelders, daughter of Arnold, Duke of Guelders. The exact date and place of his birth are debated. He became king when his father was killed at the siege of Roxburgh Castle on 3 August 1460, and he was crowned at Kelso Abbey a week later. His minority lasted almost a decade. At first his mother governed as regent, and in April 1461 the Lancastrians she had sheltered, Henry VI of England and Margaret of Anjou, gave up Berwick to the Scots in return for refuge and loans.

In July 1466 Robert, Lord Boyd, and his son Thomas seized the king while he was hunting at Linlithgow Palace and took control of the government. The Boyds arranged a marriage to Margaret, only daughter of Christian I of Denmark and Norway, whose dowry was 60,000 Rhenish guilders. When her fleet reached Leith in 1469 the Boyds fled and were convicted of treason, and James married the 13-year-old Margaret at Holyrood Abbey in July 1469. Orkney and Shetland came to Scotland through the marriage, and the reign saw Scotland reach its widest extent.

James began his personal rule in 1469. He planned costly schemes on the continent, among them a claim to Brittany that he gave up after clerical protests. In 1475 he moved against John MacDonald, Lord of the Isles, who had agreed in 1462 to the Treaty of Westminster with Edward IV of England. The Lord of the Isles was declared forfeit in December 1475, but he appeared before the king in July 1476 and the forfeiture was lifted. He lost the earldom of Ross and was reduced to a Lord of Parliament.

James faced growing criticism. Parliament complained that he did not hold the Justice Ayres in person and drew money from remissions for serious crimes, and he favoured men of low birth such as William Scheves, who became Archbishop of St Andrews. His brother John, Earl of Mar, died in prison in 1479. In 1482 his brother Alexander, Duke of Albany, tried to take the throne with an English army, which cost Scotland Berwick, and nobles imprisoned the king for a time before he regained power.

In February 1488 the fifteen-year-old heir, James, Duke of Rothesay, left Stirling Castle and became the figurehead of a rebellion led by the Earls of Angus and Argyll and the Home and Hepburn families. It ended at the Battle of Sauchieburn on 11 June 1488, where the king died, and the prince succeeded him as James IV. His reputation as Scotland's first Renaissance monarch has sometimes been exaggerated.
james-iv-of-scotland: James was born on 17 March 1473 at Stirling Castle, the eldest son of King James III and Margaret of Denmark, and was Duke of Rothesay from birth. He was educated by Archibald Whitelaw and the theologian John Ireland. Besides Scots he became fluent in Latin and Spanish, learned French, German, Flemish and Italian, and was the last Scottish monarch known to have spoken Gaelic. He became king at fifteen on 11 June 1488, when his father died at the Battle of Sauchieburn, after a rebellion in which he had been the figurehead of the rebels, and he was crowned at Scone Abbey on 24 June.

In 1491 Alexander MacDonald of Lochalsh raided Ross-shire in an attempt to recover the earldom of Ross. In consequence, a parliament in Edinburgh in May 1493 declared the title and possessions of John MacDonald, Lord of the Isles, forfeit to the Crown. James then made an expedition to the western Highlands, where local chiefs submitted, and John of Islay was brought to court with an annual pension. Parliaments met ten times from 1488 to 1496 but only three times in the remaining seventeen years, and royal income doubled over the reign. The Treaty of Ayton of 30 September 1497 agreed a seven-year truce with England, and the Treaty of Perpetual Peace followed in 1502, with James's marriage to Margaret Tudor in 1503.

He took a close interest in the navy, commissioning or acquiring at least thirty-eight ships, and naval spending became the largest single item of royal expenditure. He was a patron of the Scots poets William Dunbar, Walter Kennedy and Gavin Douglas, backed the foundation of King's College, Aberdeen, and passed the education act of 1496, which required the eldest sons of barons and substantial freeholders to attend grammar school. His court was cosmopolitan and included Africans, among them two women mentioned in the treasurer's accounts in 1504. In 1507 Pope Julius II granted him the title Protector and Defender of the Christian Faith.

When Henry VIII invaded France in 1513 as part of the Holy League, James chose the Auld Alliance with France over the Perpetual Peace and led an army of some 42,000 across the Tweed around 22 August. He took Norham, Etal and Ford castles, and on 8 September faced the English under Thomas Howard, Earl of Surrey, on Branxton Hill. James and many of his nobles were killed at the Battle of Flodden on 9 September 1513. His body was identified the next day, taken to Berwick-upon-Tweed and embalmed. He was the last monarch in Great Britain to be killed in battle and was succeeded by his son James V.
james-joyce: James Joyce was born on 2 February 1882 in Rathgar, Dublin, the eldest of ten surviving siblings. His father, John Stanislaus Joyce, was appointed rate collector by Dublin Corporation in 1887, but his unpredictable finances made family life chaotic. Joyce attended Clongowes Wood College and Belvedere College, and in 1898 enrolled at University College, Dublin, to study English, French and Italian, graduating in 1902. There he met the scholasticism of Thomas Aquinas, which influenced his thought for the rest of his life. He lapsed from the Catholic Church early, though his work is deeply influenced by Catholicism.

In October 1904 Joyce and Nora Barnacle went into self-imposed exile. He taught English in Pola and then Trieste, then part of Austria-Hungary, worked for eight months as a correspondence clerk in a Roman bank, and lived in Trieste until 1915, publishing Chamber Music and Dubliners there. He spent most of the First World War in Zurich, supported by a stipend that Pound and Yeats helped arrange and by regular sums from the editor Harriet Shaw Weaver, who supported him for the rest of his life.

In 1920 he moved to Paris, his main home for twenty years. Sylvia Beach, who ran the bookshop Shakespeare and Company, became one of his publishers. Ulysses was first published in Paris in 1922; its publication in the United Kingdom and the United States was prohibited as obscene, and copies were smuggled in and pirated until the mid-1930s, when publication became legal. He began Finnegans Wake in 1923, and suffered increasingly severe eye problems.

When Germany occupied France in 1940, Joyce moved back to Zurich. He underwent surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer on 11 January 1941 and died on 13 January, aged 58. Though he spent most of his adult life abroad, his fiction centres on Dublin. Ulysses is a model for fiction writers, and Finnegans Wake has become one of the key texts for French post-structuralism. His work and life are marked each year on 16 June, known as Bloomsday, in Dublin and in a growing number of other cities.
james-madison: James Madison Jr. was born on 16 March 1751 (5 March 1750 in the Old Style calendar) at the Belle Grove plantation near Port Conway in the Colony of Virginia. His father was a tobacco planter who, with an estimated 100 slaves and a 5,000-acre plantation, was among the largest landowners in Virginia's Piedmont. Madison joined the Patriots in 1774, believing that Parliament had overstepped its bounds in taxing the colonies,. With Thomas Jefferson he drafted the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, passed in 1786, which guaranteed freedom of religion and disestablished the Church of England.

Troubled in the 1780s by the weakness of the central government and the disunity of the states, Madison helped organise the Constitutional Convention, and his Virginia Plan was the basis of its deliberations. He became a leader of the movement to ratify the Constitution and wrote essays of The Federalist Papers with Alexander Hamilton and John Jay. Elected to the House of Representatives in 1789 after a hard contest against James Monroe, he introduced the Bill of Rights on 8 June 1789 after studying more than two hundred amendments proposed at the state ratifying conventions.

In the 1790s he opposed Hamilton's economic programme, including the First Bank of the United States, arguing that the Constitution gave Congress no power to create it, and with Jefferson he organised the Democratic–Republican Party. He served as Jefferson's Secretary of State from 1801 to 1809 and was elected president in 1808.

As president he tried to play Britain and France against each other over attacks on American shipping, and when this failed he led the country into the War of 1812. Madison was re-elected in 1812. The war ended inconclusively in 1815, but many Americans saw it as a second war of independence, and he presided over the creation of the Second Bank of the United States and the Tariff of 1816. During his presidency the United States acquired 26,000,000 acres from Native American tribes through treaties or war.

Madison retired to his plantation, Montpelier, in 1817,. Madison owned over one hundred slaves, and his views on slavery were conflicted throughout his life; his will freed none of them. He died of congestive heart failure at Montpelier on 28 June 1836, aged 85, and was one of the last prominent members of the Revolutionary generation to die. Historians regard him as one of the most significant of the Founding Fathers.
james-monroe: James Monroe was born on 28 April 1758 in Westmoreland County in the Colony of Virginia, the son of Andrew Spence Monroe, a craftsman who took part in protests against the Stamp Act, and Elizabeth Jones. In early 1776 he left college and joined the 3rd Virginia Regiment of the Continental Army as a lieutenant. At the Battle of Trenton he suffered a severed artery and nearly died; George Washington cited him for bravery and promoted him to captain. From 1780 to 1783 he studied law under Thomas Jefferson.

Monroe sat in the Congress of the Confederation from November 1783, where he helped to write the Northwest Ordinance. He opposed the ratification of the Constitution, and in 1790 was elected to the Senate. Washington appointed him minister to France in 1794 but recalled him in 1796. He was governor of Virginia from 1799 to 1802, and as Jefferson's envoy he helped to negotiate the Louisiana Purchase. He fell out with James Madison over the Monroe–Pinkney Treaty, but in April 1811 became Madison's Secretary of State, and in the War of 1812 also served as Secretary of War.

He defeated the Federalist Rufus King in 1816, and his inauguration on 4 March 1817 opened what was called the Era of Good Feelings, as the Federalists collapsed; in 1820 he was re-elected unopposed. He signed the Missouri Compromise, and in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819 the United States secured Florida and a border across the continent.

After his term ended in 1825 Monroe lived at Oak Hill in Aldie, Virginia, and was beset by financial difficulties. His wife Elizabeth died in 1830, and he moved to New York City, where he died on 4 July 1831. Monroe owned dozens of enslaved people, and sold property, including enslaved people, to pay debts. Polls of historians tend to rank him as an above-average president. He was a member of the American Colonization Society, and Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, is named after him. He was the last president to wear the powdered wig and knee-breeches of the late 18th century.
james-the-great: James was born into a family of Jewish fishermen on the Sea of Galilee. His parents were Zebedee and Salome, and Salome was a sister of Mary, the mother of Jesus, which made James a cousin of Jesus. He was the brother of John the Apostle. He is called the Greater to distinguish him from the other apostle James, the Lesser, the term meaning older or taller rather than more important. The Synoptic Gospels state that James and John were preparing to fish with their father by the shore when Jesus called them to follow him.

James, John and Peter formed an informal triumvirate among the Twelve. They were the only apostles present at three occasions of the ministry of Jesus: the raising of Jairus' daughter, the transfiguration and the agony in the Garden of Gethsemane. The brothers were nicknamed Boanerges, the Sons of Thunder. James and John, or in another tradition their mother, asked Jesus for seats on his right and left in his glory, and Jesus rebuked them.

The Acts of the Apostles records that Herod the king, usually identified with Herod Agrippa, had James executed by the sword. He was the first of the apostles to be martyred. The Armenian Apostolic Cathedral of St. James in the Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem is the traditional site, and his head is believed to lie under the altar of its Chapel of Saint James the Great.

The Historia Compostelana, commissioned by Diego Gelmírez in the 12th century, sets out the legend as it was believed at Compostela. James preached in Hispania as well as the Holy Land, and after his execution his followers carried his body by sea to Padrón in Galicia and overland to Santiago de Compostela. The Compostela tradition places the discovery of the relics in the 9th century, when Pelayo found them in the Libredon forest in the time of Bishop Theodemir and King Alfonso II. The pilgrimage route known as the Way of St. James began to form from that century.

A later tradition has him appear in battle for the Christian army at Clavijo, as Santiago Matamoros, and Spanish Christian armies took his name as a battle cry. The military Order of Santiago was founded in Spain in the 12th century. His emblem is the scallop shell, which pilgrims wore, and his feast day is 25 July.
james-vi-and-i: James was born on 19 June 1566, the only son of Mary, Queen of Scots, and Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, both great-grandchildren of Henry VII of England. He was entrusted to the Earl and Countess of Mar at Stirling Castle and crowned at the Church of the Holy Rude on 29 July 1567, at thirteen months, with John Knox preaching the sermon. Although his mother was a Catholic, he was raised as a Protestant. Four regents governed during his minority, which officially ended in 1578, though he did not fully control his government until 1583.

In Scotland James married Anne of Denmark in 1589, after sailing from Leith to fetch her when storms forced her ship to the coast of Norway. His visit to Denmark sparked an interest in witchcraft, and he attended the North Berwick witch trials. In 1597 and 1598 he wrote The True Law of Free Monarchies and Basilikon Doron, which set out the divine right of kings. He is credited with achieving most of his aims in Scotland.

Elizabeth I died early on 24 March 1603, and James was proclaimed king in London the same day. He tried to bring about a closer union of Scotland and England, but they stayed separate states with their own parliaments, judiciaries and laws, and from 20 October 1604 he styled himself King of Great Britain. He faced the Gunpowder Plot, discovered on the night of 4 to 5 November 1605, and quarrels with the English Parliament. After the plot he sanctioned harsh measures against English Catholics, including the Oath of Allegiance, though he was conciliatory to those who took it. He sponsored the translation of the Bible later named for him, and a 1604 revision of the Book of Common Prayer.

In his last years James suffered from arthritis, gout and kidney stones and was often seriously ill. He died on 27 March 1625. His reign in Scotland, of 57 years and 246 days, was the longest of any Scottish monarch. He was widely mourned, and his people had enjoyed peace and comparatively low taxation under him. He had often neglected government for the hunt, and his reliance on favourites at a scandal-ridden court weakened the image of monarchy that Elizabeth I had built. The courtier Anthony Weldon is credited with the epithet the wisest fool in Christendom.
james-watt: James Watt was born in Greenock, Renfrewshire, in January 1736, the eldest of the five surviving children of Agnes Muirhead and James Watt, a shipwright, ship owner and contractor who served as Greenock's chief baillie in 1751. The family's wealth came in part from his father's trading in slaves and slave-produced goods. His parents were Presbyterians and strong Covenanters, but he later became a deist. He was educated at home by his mother and then at Greenock Grammar School, where he showed an aptitude for mathematics while Latin and Greek failed to interest him. After leaving school he worked in his father's workshops, and when his father's ventures failed he left for Glasgow to find employment as a mathematical instrument maker.

In 1759 his friend John Robison called his attention to steam as a source of motive power. The Newcomen engine had been used for almost fifty years to pump water from mines and had hardly changed. Watt began to experiment, though he had never seen an operating steam engine, and came to realise the importance of latent heat, which his friend Joseph Black had discovered years before. His insight was that contemporary engines wasted energy by repeatedly cooling and reheating the cylinder, and he introduced the separate condenser to avoid this. Eventually he adapted the engine to produce rotary motion, which greatly broadened its use beyond pumping water.

Watt had great financial difficulties until he entered a partnership with Matthew Boulton in 1775. The first engines were installed in commercial enterprises in 1776, and for the next five years he installed more, mostly in Cornwall. Boulton and Watt charged an annual payment equal to one-third of the value of the coal saved compared with a Newcomen engine. Mine owners in Cornwall became convinced that his patent could not be enforced and withheld payments, and Watt had to go to court. The Soho Foundry formally opened in 1796, and in 1800 Watt retired, the year his fundamental patent and the partnership expired.

The story that Watt was inspired by a boiling kettle is probably apocryphal, possibly created by his son James Watt Jr.; Watt did not invent the steam engine but improved the existing Newcomen engine. He also devised a letter copying machine and studied chemistry, finding that a solution of chlorine could bleach textiles. In retirement he built machines for copying sculptures, which he never patented. He was a member of the Lunar Society of Birmingham. The chemist Humphry Davy said that those who considered him only a practical mechanic formed an erroneous idea of him, since he was equally distinguished as a natural philosopher and a chemist. He died on 25 August 1819, and the SI unit of power, the watt, is named after him.
jamestown: Jamestown stood on the north-east bank of the James River, about 4 km south-west of present-day Williamsburg, in what later became James City County. The Virginia Company of London established it as James Fort on 4 May 1607 O.S., which is 14 May 1607 N.S. It followed earlier failed English attempts at colonisation, including the Roanoke Colony of 1585. The colonists chose a river island to avoid Spanish naval patrols, but it was infested with mosquitoes, lacked drinkable water and was used by the Paspahegh people. The fleet, under Captain Christopher Newport, consisted of the Susan Constant, Discovery and Godspeed.

Only 60 of the original 214 settlers survived the winter of 1609–1610, known as the Starving Time. Progress in the first years was uneven, owing to the aristocratic backgrounds of many colonists, a historic drought and the communal organisation of work. In 1612 tobacco from the West Indies was cultivated successfully, which led to an economic boom for the colony and for England. By 1613 Sir Thomas Dale had assigned 3-acre plots to the early planters, and the settlers began to spread onto land belonging to local native peoples.

Jamestown was the colonial capital from 1616 to 1699. In 1619 it saw the first legislative assembly in the New World, a labour strike and the first recorded African slaves in the Virginia colony, who most likely worked in the tobacco fields. A native uprising in 1622 devastated the surrounding settlements, but the capital was warned in time. In 1624 King James revoked the Virginia Company's charter and Virginia became a crown colony. Jamestown was deliberately burned during Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 and rebuilt, and in 1699 the capital moved to Williamsburg. The settlement then declined, and the church was abandoned in the 1750s.

Jamestown is now an archaeological site. The remains of the original 1607 fort, thought to have been lost to the river, were discovered in 1996 by the Jamestown Rediscovery project. Historic Jamestowne, run jointly by the National Park Service and Preservation Virginia, has the fort site, a seventeenth-century church tower and a museum of the artifacts found. Nearby, Jamestown Settlement is a living-history museum with replicas of the three ships. Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown form the Historic Triangle of Colonial Virginia.
jami: Nūr ad-Dīn 'Abd ar-Rahmān Jāmī was born on 7 November 1414 at Kharjerd in Khorasan to a Persian family. His father, Nizām al-Dīn Ahmad, had come from Dasht in the district of Isfahan, so his early pen name was Dashti; he later chose Jami for two reasons he gave in a poem, his birthplace of Jam and the Sufi Sheikh-ul-Islam Ahmad Jam. A few years after his birth the family moved to Herat, where he studied philosophy, mathematics, rhetoric, logic and Arabic and Persian literature at the Nizamiyya, with his father, also a Sufi, as his first teacher. He completed his studies at Samarkand and made a pilgrimage that raised his reputation across the Persian world.

In Herat Jami held an important position at the Timurid court and was a mentor and friend of the Turkic poet Alisher Navoi. He belonged to the Naqshbandi Sufi order and the school of Ibn Arabi, though he did not always follow it: on the dependence of God and creatures he wrote, "We and Thou are not separate from each other, but we need Thee, whereas Thou dost not need us." He became a Sufi shaykh in 1453 and defined terms such as sainthood and the levels of tawhid.

He wrote about eighty-seven books and letters. His major poetical work is the Haft Awrang (Seven Thrones), seven long masnavis, by his own admission influenced by Nizami, among them Salaman va Absal, an allegory of the stages of the Sufi path, and Yusuf and Zulaykha, based on the Quran. He also wrote the Kherad-name in the tradition of the Alexander Romance, three collections of lyric poems, the Nafahat al-Uns, a collection of biographies of Sufi saints, and the Baharestan, modelled on Saadi's Gulestan, for his surviving son Zia-ol-din Yusef. His commentary on the Arabic grammar Al-Kafiya was a staple of Ottoman madrasa curricula.

Jami was living in Herat at the end of his life. Dates for his death vary, but most sources give November 1492. The prince of Herat conducted his funeral, which large numbers attended. His poetry was popular across the Islamic East, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, and his works were used in schools from Samarqand to Istanbul and in the Mughal Empire. Babur, in the Baburnama, called him the foremost authority of the age in all of the sciences, and later Mughal emperors made versions of Yusuf and Zulaykha. Jami himself politely declined an invitation to settle in the Deccan.
jammu: Jammu lies on the Tawi river among low ridges in the Shivalik hills, with the Shivalik range to the north, east and southeast and the Trikuta Range to the northwest, at an average elevation of 300 metres. The old city overlooks the river from its north bank, and the newer neighbourhoods spread over the south bank. According to local tradition it was named after its founder Raja Jambulochan, who is believed to have ruled in the 9th century, and the tradition says the city is 3,000 years old, a claim historians do not support.

According to the Tarikh-i-Azmi, Jammu came into existence around 900 CE, and the state of Durgara, from which the names Duggar and Dogra come, is attested from about the same time. Its rulers are repeatedly mentioned in Kalhana's Rajatarangini. Timur's chronicles name Jammu, since he returned to Samarkand through it after invading Delhi in 1398. Babur's chronicles describe it as a powerful state of the Punjab hills ruled by Manhas Rajputs. Akbar brought the hill kingdoms under Mughal suzerainty, though their kings kept considerable autonomy, and the Mughal empire treated them as allies and partners.

After Mughal power declined in the 18th century the Jammu state under Raja Dhruv Dev of the Jamwal family asserted its supremacy among the Dugar states. Its height came under his successor Raja Ranjit Dev, who ruled from 1728 to 1780 and promoted religious freedom and security, which drew craftsmen and traders to settle there. Towards the end of his rule the Sikh misls gained ground; around 1770 the Bhangi misl forced Ranjit Dev to become a tributary, and his successor Brij Lal Dev was defeated by Mahan Singh of the Sukerchakia misl, who sacked Jammu.

In 1808 Ranjit Singh, son of Mahan Singh, annexed it to the Sikh Empire. In 1818 Kishore Singh, father of Gulab Singh, was appointed ruler of the Jammu principality, which began the Jamwal or Dogra dynasty that came to rule the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under British suzerainty.

Jammu is the winter capital of the union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, to which the offices move from Srinagar from November to April. It was the winter capital of the princely state from 1846 to 1952 and the capital of Jammu Province. The city is the cultural and economic centre of the Jammu division, and is about 600 kilometres from New Delhi.
jamsetji-tata: Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata was born on 3 March 1839 in Navsari, to a respectable but poor family of Zoroastrian priests. His father, Nusserwanji Ratanji Tata, had broken with the priestly tradition to become the first businessman in the family. Jamsetji's mother tongue was Gujarati. His parents saw that he was gifted in mental arithmetic, and he joined his father in Bombay at the age of 14 and enrolled at Elphinstone College, completing his studies as a Green Scholar. He married Hirabai Daboo while still a student. After graduating in 1858 he joined his father's export-trading firm and helped set up branches in Japan, China, Europe and the United States.

His father sent him to China to learn how business was done there, including the opium trade. Tata saw instead that the cotton industry was booming. He worked in his father's company until he was 29 and then founded a trading company in 1868 with ₹21,000 of capital. In 1869 he bought a bankrupt oil mill at Chinchpokli, converted it to a cotton mill called Alexandra Mill, and sold it two years later at a profit. In 1874 he floated the Central India Spinning, Weaving, and Manufacturing Company in Nagpur, and people in Bombay, the Cottonopolis of India, scorned the unconventional choice of place.

In 1885 a company he floated in Pondicherry to distribute Indian textiles to nearby French colonies free of duty failed for lack of demand. He then bought the Dharamsi Mills at Kurla, resold them, and bought the Advance Mills in Ahmedabad, named for its up-to-date machinery. He supported the principles of Swadeshism before the Swadeshi movement began in 1905, and named a new Bombay mill the Swadeshi Mill, meant to produce cloth to match Manchester's. He tried to improve the cultivation of cotton in India and was the first to introduce the ring spindle into his mills, which replaced the throstle.

Tata set himself four aims: an iron and steel company, a world-class learning institution, a unique hotel and a hydroelectric plant. Only the hotel was completed in his lifetime, when the Taj Mahal Hotel opened on the Colaba waterfront in Mumbai on 3 December 1903. His successors achieved the other three. He gave generously to education and healthcare. He fell seriously ill on a business trip to Germany in 1900 and died at Bad Nauheim on 19 May 1904, and he was buried in the Parsi burial ground in Brookwood Cemetery, Woking, England. His sons Dorab and Ratan continued his work, and Dorab succeeded him as chair of the Tata Group. Jawaharlal Nehru called him a One-Man Planning Commission.
jamshedpur: Jamshedpur lies at the confluence of the Swarnarekha and Kharkai rivers in the south of Jharkhand, bordered by Odisha and West Bengal, and is surrounded by the forested Dalma Hills. It is part of the larger Chota Nagpur Plateau, at an average elevation of 135 metres. The modern city was built over the village of Sakchi. Its central part includes old neighbourhoods such as Sakchi, Bistupur and Golmuri, while the south-east is largely industrial and residential. It is also known as Tatanagar.

At the end of the nineteenth century Jamshedji Tata met steelmakers in Pittsburgh to obtain the most advanced technology for his plant, and at the turn of the twentieth century he asked the geologist Charles Page Perin to find a site for India's first steel plant. The search for a place rich in iron, coal, limestone and water began in April 1904. His son Dorabji Tata chose the location at Sakchi, the project began in 1908 and the plant was operating by 1912. Lord Chelmsford named the city Jamshedpur in 1919, in honour of Jamshedji, whose birthday, 3 March, is marked as Founder's Day.

During the First World War Tata Steel supplied rail and steel to British military campaigns in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Salonica and East Africa. In the Second World War the city was a high-value target, and British and American troops and air bases were stationed in the region. On 1 January 1948 the Orissa Military Police opened fire on a crowd of over 50,000 at Kharsawan, who were protesting against its merger; official records state 35 deaths, while other sources give figures as high as 2,000. After independence the city lay in Bihar until it became part of the new state of Jharkhand on 15 November 2000.

The 2011 census counted 629,659 people in the city and 1,337,131 in the urban agglomeration. Hindi, Bengali, Santali, Bhojpuri, Odia, Urdu and Punjabi are the main languages. Tata Steel, in the centre of the city, occupies about a fifth of its area, and Tata Motors is the second major industry. The city is called India's first planned industrial city, envisioned by an Indian, planned by an American, named by a British Viceroy and landscaped by a German botanist. Jubilee Park, of 225 acres, is decorated with lights for about a week on Founder's Day.
jan-hus: Jan Hus was born at Husinec in southern Bohemia to peasant parents; the exact date is disputed and most of what is known of his early life is unsubstantiated. He took his name from the village, and the word hus means goose in Czech. He began teaching at the University of Prague in 1398, defended propositions of John Wycliffe in public for the first time in 1399, and was ordained as a Catholic priest in 1400. He became dean of the philosophy department in 1401 and a rector of the university a year later, and in 1402 he was appointed preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel.

Hus translated Wycliffe's Trialogus into Czech and helped distribute it, even though Church authorities banned many of Wycliffe's works in 1403. From his pulpit he denounced the moral failings of clergy, bishops and even the papacy. In 1409 King Wenceslaus IV, wishing the university to stay neutral in the Western Schism, decreed that the Czech nation should have three votes and the German nation only one. The German masters and students left for Heidelberg and Leipzig, more than a thousand of them by one estimate, and spread accusations of Bohemian heresy. Hus was excommunicated and spent two years in exile.

King Sigismund arranged a general council at Constance, which opened on 1 November 1414, and Hus agreed to attend under his promise of safe-conduct. At his trial on 8 June 1415 thirty-nine sentences drawn from his books were read to him. He declared himself willing to recant if his errors were proved from the Bible, but refused to confess that he had erred. He was burned at the stake on 6 July 1415, and his ashes were thrown into the Rhine.

On 2 September 1415 a hundred nobles of Bohemia and Moravia sealed a protest against his burning. Under Jan Žižka and later Prokop the Great the Hussites defeated crusades sent against them, and the fighting ended with the Basel Compacts of 1436, which allowed Bohemia to practise its own form of Christianity. A century later as much as ninety per cent of the Czech lands' inhabitants still followed Hussite teaching. In 1999 Pope John Paul II expressed deep regret for the cruel death inflicted on Hus. His followers survive in the Moravian Church.
jan-iii-sobieski: John Sobieski was born on 17 August 1629 at Olesko, now in Ukraine, into a noble family; his father, Jakub Sobieski, was Voivode of Ruthenia and Castellan of Kraków. He studied at Kraków and then spent more than two years travelling in western Europe with his brother Marek, learning French, German and Italian. Returning in 1648 to the Khmelnytsky Uprising, he fought at the siege of Zamość and at Berestechko. Sent to the Ottoman Empire as an envoy, he learned Turkish and Tatar and studied Ottoman tactics. In the Swedish invasion known as the Deluge he briefly swore allegiance to Charles X Gustav before returning to King John II Casimir in 1656.

Sobieski became Grand Hetman of the Crown in 1668. After defeating the Ottomans at the Battle of Khotyn on 11 November 1673, he was elected king on 19 May 1674 and crowned on 2 February 1676. He inherited a country devastated by almost half a century of war, with an almost empty treasury. The Treaty of Żurawno of 1676 brought a period of peace in which he reorganised the army into regiments and increased its artillery. His plans to conquer Prussia failed, and in 1683 he allied himself with Emperor Leopold I against the Ottomans, an agreement signed on 31 March.

On 12 September 1683 Sobieski, in joint command of Polish, Austrian and German troops, attacked the Ottoman army of Kara Mustafa at Vienna. The allies numbered about 65,000 to 76,000 men against about 143,000, and in the late afternoon he led the Polish hussars in a charge down the Kahlenberg that broke the Ottoman line. The Pope hailed him as saviour of Western Christendom. The war continued within the Holy League, and the Poles gained no lasting territorial rewards.

Sobieski died of a sudden heart attack at Wilanów on 17 June 1696, after increasing illness, and was succeeded by Augustus II the Strong. He is buried in Wawel Cathedral at Kraków, with his heart in the Church of the Transfiguration in Warsaw. He is remembered in Poland as a hero king, an image strengthened by nineteenth-century literature, although he failed to reform the Commonwealth or secure the throne for his heir. He was a patron of the astronomer Johannes Hevelius, and Wilanów Palace was the first of many palaces in the Commonwealth.
jan-palach: Jan Palach was born on 11 August 1948 and attended elementary school in Všetaty, where he was an avid reader of Jules Verne. His father died when he was 13, and he was raised in part by his grandfather. He graduated from a gymnasium in Mělník in 1966, attended the Prague School of Economics, and in September 1968 transferred to the Faculty of Arts at Charles University, where he studied history and political economics. In the summer of 1967 he worked on a chicken farm in the Soviet Union, where he instigated a strike with other Czech students that reduced their working day from ten hours to eight. On 7 November 1968 he took part in a demonstration for Czech independence.

On 16 January 1969, after the Warsaw Pact invasion that crushed the reforms of Alexander Dubček's government, Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square and suffered burns over 85 percent of his body. In a letter to several public figures he demanded the abolition of censorship and a halt to the distribution of Zprávy, the newspaper of the Soviet occupying forces, and called for a general strike. The burns specialist Jaroslava Moserová, who first treated him, said that he acted against the demoralisation of Czechoslovak citizens that the occupation had caused. He died in hospital three days later.

His funeral became a major protest against the occupation. On 25 February another student, Jan Zajíc, burned himself to death at the same place, and Evžen Plocek did so at Jihlava in April. Palach was first buried at the Olšany Cemetery in Prague. As the grave became a national shrine the secret police exhumed his remains on 25 October 1973 and cremated them; his ashes were returned to the Prague grave on 25 October 1990.

Between 15 and 21 January 1989, protests in Prague ostensibly in his memory but intended as anticommunist demonstrations grew into Palach Week, which the police suppressed. It is considered one of the demonstrations that preceded the fall of communism in Czechoslovakia ten months later. A bronze cross marks the spot outside the National Museum where he fell, and Jan Palach Square in Prague is named for him.
jan-smuts: Jan Christiaan Smuts was born on 24 May 1870 at the family farm, Bovenplaats, near Malmesbury in the Cape Colony, to prosperous Afrikaner parents. As the second son he was expected to work on the farm, but when his elder brother died in 1882 he was sent to school in his place. He caught up with his contemporaries within four years, entered Victoria College, Stellenbosch, in 1886 and went on to study law at Christ's College, Cambridge, on a scholarship. He was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1894 and returned home the following year.

Smuts first supported Cecil Rhodes, but the Jameson Raid of 1895-96 outraged him, and he became state attorney of the South African Republic in Pretoria. In the Second Boer War he served first as Paul Kruger's aide in Pretoria and from mid-1900 under Koos de la Rey in the Western Transvaal, where he excelled at hit-and-run warfare. He helped negotiate the Treaty of Vereeniging in 1902. In May 1904 he joined other former Transvaal generals in founding Het Volk, with Louis Botha as leader and himself as deputy. After the fall of the Conservative government in December 1905 he and Botha went to London and won responsible government for the Transvaal.

In the Union of South Africa of 1910 Botha became prime minister and Smuts held the ministries of the Interior, Mines and Defence. In the First World War he formed the Union Defence Force, put down the Maritz Rebellion, helped conquer German South-West Africa and in 1916 took charge of the campaign in German East Africa. He sat in the Imperial War Cabinet from 1917 and at the Paris Peace Conference helped shape the League of Nations. He succeeded Botha as prime minister in 1919 and lost office in 1924 to J. B. M. Hertzog's National Party.

Smuts returned as deputy prime minister in a coalition with Hertzog, and when Hertzog's motion for neutrality was defeated by 80 votes to 67 in 1939 he became prime minister again and took South Africa into the Second World War. He was made a field marshal on 24 May 1941. He wrote the first draft of the preamble to the United Nations Charter and signed the charters of both the League of Nations and the United Nations. His book Holism and Evolution (1926) set out the concept of holism. He supported racial segregation, and the National Party won the 1948 election, after which apartheid was introduced.
In 1948 he became Chancellor of the University of Cambridge. He suffered a coronary thrombosis on 29 May 1950 and died of a heart attack at his farm, Doornkloof, near Pretoria, on 11 September 1950.
jan-van-eyck: Neither the date nor the place of Jan van Eyck's birth is documented; he was identified in the late sixteenth century as born in Maaseik, and his name is thought to derive from it. The first record of him comes from the court of John of Bavaria at The Hague, where between 1422 and 1424 payments were made to Meyster Jan den malre (Master Jan the painter), a court painter with the rank of valet de chambre who had one and then two assistants. He helped redecorate the Binnenhof palace.

After John's death in 1425 he became court artist and diplomat to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy. In 1428 he went to Lisbon to discuss a marriage contract between the duke and Isabella of Portugal, and on 18 October 1427 he attended a banquet in his honour at Tournai, where Robert Campin and Rogier van der Weyden were also present. A court salary freed him from commissioned work and gave him artistic freedom. He settled in Bruges, bought a house and around 1432 married Margaret, who was 15 years younger.

About 20 surviving paintings are confidently attributed to him, all dated between 1432 and 1439, and ten are signed with a variation of his motto ALS ICH KAN (As I Can), a pun on his name, which first appeared in 1433 on Portrait of a Man in a Turban. The Ghent Altarpiece, painted for Jodocus Vijdts and Elisabeth Borluut, was started before 1426 and completed by 1432. His high point is generally placed between 1434 and 1436, with the Madonna of Chancellor Rolin, the Lucca Madonna and the Virgin and Child with Canon van der Paele.

In portraits he used layers of thin translucent glazes that gave a rich depth of colour and vivid likenesses. He often signed and dated his frames, painting them to look like imitation stone, and many of his panels carry inscriptions in Greek, Latin or Dutch. Giorgio Vasari's claim that he invented oil painting is now considered an oversimplification.

Jan van Eyck died in Bruges on 9 July 1441 and was buried in the graveyard of the Church of St Donatian. Philip the Good made a one-off payment to his widow equal to the painter's annual salary. His unfinished works were completed by his workshop, which was run by his brother Lambert, who had the body moved into St Donatian's early in 1442. In 1454 Bartolomeo Facio named him the leading painter of his day, and his style was widely adopted by Rogier van der Weyden, Petrus Christus and Hans Memling.
jan-zizka: Žižka was born in the village of Trocnov in the Kingdom of Bohemia, into the lower gentry, which owned little estate. His birth date is unknown. A document of 3 April 1378 names a Johannes dictus Zizka de Trocnov as a witness to a marriage contract, and from it historians assume a birth around 1360, though the historian Tomek and others thought that man might have been the general's father. According to the Polish chronicler Jan Długosz, he served as a mercenary on the Polish-Lithuanian side at the Battle of Grunwald on 15 July 1410. A later report says he served Sophia of Bavaria, wife of Wenceslas IV, as chamberlain; his activity in the years 1411 to 1419 is not entirely certain.

Žižka first appears prominently on 30 July 1419, when he joined a Hussite procession led by the priest Jan Želivský in Prague. The crowd stormed the New Town hall and threw councillors from the windows, the First Defenestration of Prague, which is regarded as the start of the Hussite revolution. Žižka then left Prague, defeated partisans of King Sigismund at Sudoměř on 25 March 1420, the first pitched battle of the Hussite wars, and went to Tábor, where he became one of four captains of the people. Pope Martin V proclaimed a crusade on 17 March 1420.

Žižka helped develop the wagon fort. Carts were joined wheel to wheel in a square or circle, with a ditch in front, each crewed by 16 to 22 soldiers, including crossbowmen, handgunners and men with pikes or flails. Artillery provoked the enemy knights into attacking, and shooters aimed first at the horses. He was the first European commander to manoeuvre with medium-calibre cannon mounted on carts.

At Kutná Hora at the end of 1421 he was trapped but broke out to Kolín, and on 6 January 1422 defeated Sigismund's army at Nebovidy. Německý Brod was stormed on 10 January, and its defenders were put to the sword contrary to his orders.

In 1423 dissent among the Hussites led to civil war. As leader of the Taborites, Žižka defeated the men of Prague and the Utraquist nobles at Hořice on 20 April 1423, and the Utraquists under Bořek at Strachov on 4 August. He died on 11 October 1424. A monument to him stands on Vítkov Hill in Prague, and he is regarded as a Czech national hero.
jana-gana-mana: The song's lyrics first appeared in five stanzas in the Bengali magazine Tattwabodhini Patrika, the official publication of the Brahmo Samaj, of which Tagore was then editor, under the title Bharat Bhagya Bidhata. Tagore composed the melody himself in the raga Alhaiya Bilaval, possibly with some help from his musician grand-nephew Dinendranath Tagore.

It was first sung in public on the second day of the Indian National Congress session in Calcutta on 27 December 1911, by Tagore's niece in her school assembly. It was followed in January 1912 at the annual event of the Adi Brahmo Samaj, but remained largely unknown except to readers of the Brahmo journal. On 28 February 1919 Tagore sang it at the Besant Theosophical College in Madanapalle, where Margaret Cousins, the vice-principal, preserved it in Western notation from notes he provided, and where he made his own English translation, The Morning Song of India.

The poem is composed in Sadhu Bhasha, a heavily Sanskritised literary register of Bengali. Its five verses make up a hymn; only the first was adopted as the national anthem. A formal rendition takes about 52 seconds, and a shortened version of the first and last lines takes about 20 seconds.

Its first stanza names the provinces that were under direct British rule, among them Punjab, Sindh, Gujarat, Maratha, Dravida, Utkala and Bengal, but none of the princely states. Defenders hold that Tagore named only border regions in order to include all of India.

Subhas Chandra Bose chose the song as a national anthem while in Germany, and on 11 September 1942 the Hamburg Radio Symphony Orchestra played it as India's anthem at the founding meeting of the German-Indian Society. The Constituent Assembly closed its midnight session on 14 August 1947 with a unanimous performance, and adopted the first stanza as the National Anthem on 24 January 1950.

A dispute arose from reports in the British Indian press that a song of welcome to the Emperor had been sung at the 1911 Congress. Many historians hold the reports mistaken, because a different Hindi song, Badshah Humara, praised George V at the same session, and the nationalist press and the official Congress report distinguished the two. Tagore wrote in 1937 and 1939 that the Lord of Destiny of the song could never be George V or any other George. He had renounced a knighthood in 1919 in protest over the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
jane-austen: Jane Austen was born on 16 December 1775 in Steventon, Hampshire. Her father, George Austen, was the rector of the Anglican parishes of Steventon and Deane. He came from an old and wealthy family of wool merchants, but his own branch fell into poverty as each generation's eldest sons received the inheritances, and he was orphaned as a child. At sixteen he entered St John's College, Oxford, where he most likely met Cassandra Leigh, who came from the prominent Leigh family.

In 1809 her brother Edward offered his mother and sisters the use of a large cottage in Chawton, and Jane, Cassandra and their mother moved there on 7 July 1809. Life was quieter there than at any time since the family's move to Bath in 1800.

Austen wrote major novels before the age of 22 but was not published until she was 35. Like many women authors of her time she published anonymously. The ideal roles for a woman were then wife and mother, and a woman who wished to be a full-time writer was felt to be degrading her femininity. Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814) and Emma (1815) were moderate successes but did not bring her public fame in her lifetime.

Sir Walter Scott wrote an anonymous review of Emma in 1815, praising her realism. She died on 18 July 1817. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published after her death, and her brother Henry Austen's Biographical Note, dated December 1817, first identified her as the author of the novels. She left unfinished the novel Sanditon.

Austen's six novels implicitly interpret and criticise the English landed gentry at the end of the 18th century. Her plots often explore the dependence of women on marriage for social standing and economic security. Her works critique the sentimental novels of the second half of the 18th century and are part of the transition to 19th-century literary realism. Critics have praised her social commentary, wit and irony.

In 1832 Richard Bentley bought the remaining copyrights to her novels and in October 1833 released the first collected edition, in his Standard Novels series. Her novels have been continuously in print since. Her nephew published A Memoir of Jane Austen in 1869.
janissaries: The Janissary Corps was formed in the 14th century, either under Murad I or under his father Orhan. The Ottoman government took a tax of one-fifth on all slaves taken in war, and from this pool of men the sultans built a personal army loyal only to themselves. From the 1380s to 1648 the corps was filled through the devşirme, a levy of boys, predominantly Balkan Christians, who were enslaved, circumcised by force and converted to Islam. The levy was abolished in 1648. Jews were never subject to it.

A boy was first sent to a Turkish family in the provinces to learn Turkish and the customs of Ottoman society, and was then trained in the acemi oğlan, or cadet, school in the capital, where the brightest were selected for the palace institution of the Enderun. Janissaries lived in strict discipline in nearly monastic conditions and were forbidden to marry until retirement, typically in their forties. The devşirme was deeply resented among Christians in the Balkans, and in Serbian, Greek and Bulgarian memory it became one of the most enduring symbols of Ottoman rule.

Janissaries were kapıkulları, door servants of the sultan, neither freedmen nor ordinary slaves. They wore distinctive uniforms, lived in barracks, marched to the music of the mehter band and received regular salaries and pensions. The corps was divided into orta, or battalions, led by a commander called the ağa. Under Suleiman I there were 165 orta, rising to 196, in three sub-corps: the cemaat, the bölük and the sekban. A semi-autonomous corps was based in Algiers.

In the classical period the Janissaries were only about a tenth of the Ottoman army, the provincial cavalry being the main force. They numbered about 1,000 in the 14th century and about 6,000 in 1475, and from the 1530s the corps expanded, to about 40,000 men by 1609. They began adopting firearms in the early to mid 1400s and in 1605 became one of the first European armies to use rotating lines of volley fire. They took part in the capture of Constantinople in 1453.

In the late 16th century a sultan gave in to pressure and allowed Janissaries' sons to join, a practice forbidden for 200 years, and by the 17th century civilians bought their way in for the status it gave. Janissaries came to own land and businesses, mutinied, dictated policy and changed sultans by palace coups, and they resisted modernisation of the army. Mahmud II abolished the corps in 1826 in the Auspicious Incident, in which 6,000 or more were executed. Janissary music influenced Mozart and Beethoven, and the mehter band was organised again in 1952 under the Istanbul Military Museum.
janos-kadar: János Kádár was born out of wedlock on 26 May 1912 in Fiume, now Rijeka, to the servant Borbála Csermanek and the soldier János Krezinger. His mother found work in Budapest, and he met his father only once, in 1960. His first meeting with Marxist literature came in 1928, when he won a junior chess competition and received Friedrich Engels's Anti-Dühring as the prize. He was the first to be dismissed when the Great Depression struck Hungary, and by his own account he joined the Communist Party in 1931.

Kádár became First Secretary of the illegal party before the war. In 1936 he feigned its dissolution and renamed it the Peace Party to throw the police off its trail; the plan failed, and the Moscow-based Hungarian Communists under Mátyás Rákosi condemned it. After the war he sat on the Politburo, and from 1948 to 1950 he was Interior Minister. In 1951 he was imprisoned by the government of Rákosi and released in 1954 by the reformist Prime Minister Imre Nagy.

On 25 October 1956, two days after the Hungarian Revolution began, Kádár replaced Ernő Gerő as General Secretary and joined Nagy's government. A week later he broke with Nagy over the decision to withdraw from the Warsaw Pact. The Soviet leadership decided in early November to crush the revolution by force, and after the intervention Kádár was selected to lead the country. He ordered Nagy to be executed.

Kádár judged that breaking away from the Communist bloc was impossible. From the early 1960s he lifted the harshest of Rákosi's controls on speech and movement, eased limits on cultural life and tolerated samizdat publications to a greater extent than other bloc leaders did. An amnesty in 1963 released most remaining prisoners. He allowed collective-farm members large private plots, raised trade with Western Europe and favoured consumer goods, in what became known as Goulash Communism. He called himself a toiler for compromise.

On 22 May 1988 he resigned as General Secretary, under pressure, amid economic difficulties and ill health; Károly Grósz succeeded him. He lost his remaining posts in May 1989 and died on 6 July 1989. His legacy remains disputed in Hungary: supporters stress peace, job security and social protection, while critics hold that the country remained a dictatorship and a Soviet satellite.
january-uprising: Despite the Russian Empire's defeat in the Crimean War, Alexander II warned the Poles in 1856 to forget any dreams. Two currents emerged in the Kingdom of Poland. The Whites, liberal-conservative and mostly landowners, centred on Andrzej Zamoyski, hoped for an orderly return to the constitutional status before 1830. The Reds, a democratic movement of peasants, workers and some clergy, wanted the peasantry freed unconditionally. In February 1861 the Russian army attacked a demonstration in Warsaw, killing five, and on 8 April Russian fire killed 200 and wounded 500.

Aleksander Wielopolski, head of civil administration, brought forward to January 1863 the conscription of young Polish activists into the Imperial Russian Army for 20 years of service, hoping to derail the national movement. It sparked the uprising he had meant to avoid, and many young men fled to the forests.

The uprising began on 22 January 1863, organised by the clandestine Central National Committee and then by the Polish National Government. About 10,000 men rallied at first, mostly city workers and minor clerks, with younger sons of the poorer szlachta and lower priests. The insurgents fought as lightly armed guerrilla bands that avoided large battles. On 1 February 1863 the uprising spread to the former Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and by spring it reached the Kiev Governorate. France, Britain and Austria did not intervene militarily.

Disagreement between Whites and Reds weakened coordination, and the peasantry could be mobilised only where Polish units dominated. Romuald Traugutt took command on 17 October 1863. On 27 December 1863 he decreed that peasants would be granted the land they worked, but the policy came too late, since Russia had already begun offering peasants parcels of land. Alexander II abolished serfdom in Poland in 1864.

According to official Russian information, 396 people were executed and 18,672 exiled to Siberia, and over 60,000 people were imprisoned and exiled from Poland to distant regions of Russia. Whole villages and towns were burned. The authorities confiscated 1,660 estates in Poland and 1,794 in Lithuania, ended the remaining autonomy of the Kingdom of Poland, and restricted the official use of Polish. Mikhail Muravyov, called the Hangman, supervised hangings, and Count Fyodor Berg pursued Russification.

The uprising failed militarily but became a symbol of continuing resistance. In the 1860s and after, two movements grew out of it, the Polish Socialist Party under Józef Piłsudski and the National Democracy movement under Roman Dmowski. Many turned to organic work and self-improvement.
japan: Japan is an island country in East Asia, made up of 14,125 islands that stretch over 3,000 kilometres along the Pacific coast of Asia. The five main islands, from north to south, are Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and Okinawa. About 75% of the terrain is mountainous and heavily forested, so the population is concentrated on the coastal plains. Japan lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire and is prone to earthquakes, tsunami and volcanic eruptions; the 1923 Tokyo earthquake killed over 140,000 people, and the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake triggered a large tsunami.

The first known habitation dates to the Upper Paleolithic. The Jōmon period began around 14,500 BCE, and the Yayoi people later entered the archipelago from the Korean Peninsula, bringing wet-rice farming and metallurgy. According to legend, Emperor Jimmu founded a kingdom in central Japan in 660 BCE. Japan first appears in written history in the Chinese Book of Han, completed in 111 CE. Buddhism was introduced from Baekje in 552, and in 645 the Taika Reforms aimed at greater centralisation of power in the imperial court, on the model of China.

From the 12th century actual power was held by military aristocrats known as shōgun and feudal lords called daimyō. After the Kamakura and Ashikaga shogunates and a century of warring states, the Tokugawa shogunate unified the country in 1600 and implemented an isolationist foreign policy. An American fleet forced Japan to open trade in 1853, which led to the end of the shogunate and the restoration of imperial power in 1868. Japan annexed Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910, invaded China in 1937 and entered World War II as an Axis power in 1941. It surrendered in 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and was under Allied occupation until 1952.

Japan has a population of nearly 123 million, and Tokyo is the capital and largest city. It is a constitutional monarchy in which the emperor's role is ceremonial, and its legislature is the bicameral National Diet. The Constitution of Japan was adopted in 1947. Minority groups include the indigenous Ainu and Ryukyuan people.
japanese-tea-ceremony: The first documented evidence of tea in Japan dates to the 9th century. An entry in the Nihon Kōki describes the Buddhist monk Eichū bringing tea back from Tang China, and in 815 he personally served sencha to Emperor Saga on an excursion at Karasaki. By imperial order in 816, tea plantations began to be cultivated in the Kinki region, though interest in tea then faded. Buddhists used tea to prevent drowsiness during long meditations.

In the 1500s Sen no Rikyū revolutionized tea culture. He redefined the rules of the tea house, tea garden, utensils and procedures, introduced a much smaller chashitsu and rustic, distorted ceramic tea bowls, and based the ceremony on the aesthetic of wabi. His great-grandchildren founded the Omotesenke, Urasenke and Mushakōjisenke schools, and the practice spread from daimyo and samurai to the general public. Zen Buddhism and Shinto also shaped it: washing the hands and mouth before the ceremony follows the Shinto purification ritual of misogi.

The ceremony is known as sadō or chadō, the way of tea, or chanoyu, and centres on the presentation of powdered green tea, matcha, a procedure called temae. Koicha, thick tea, uses about three times as much tea to the same water as usucha, thin tea, which is whipped with a bamboo whisk. A relatively simple gathering, a chakai, includes confections, thin tea and perhaps a light meal. A formal chaji usually includes a full kaiseki meal, then confections, thick tea and thin tea, and may last up to four hours.

The year is divided into the sunken hearth season, traditionally November to April, and the brazier season, May to October. Rooms are ideally tatami-floored, with a hanging scroll in the tokonoma alcove chosen for the season and occasion, and a simple flower arrangement, chabana, which Sen no Rikyū developed. Most ceremonies are conducted in kimono, whose sleeves and obi shape many of the movements.

Schools teach many styles of temae. Obon temae, a simple procedure for thin tea on a tray, is usually the first learned. Ryūrei, with host and guests seated on chairs, originated in the Urasenke school, initially for non-Japanese guests, who, it was thought, would be more comfortable that way. Ten artisans hold the title Senke Jusshoku for supplying utensils to the three main schools.

The English term Teaism was coined by Okakura Kakuzō to describe the worldview of the way of tea, not only its presentation. A separate tradition, senchadō, uses leaf tea and was introduced from China in the 17th century by Ingen, founder of the Ōbaku school of Zen, and popularized in the 18th century by the Ōbaku monk Baisao, who sold tea in Kyoto.
jaroslav-hasek: Jaroslav Hašek was born on 30 April 1883. His father Josef, a mathematics teacher, died early, and poverty forced his mother to move the family more than fifteen times. In 1897, as a student, he took part in anti-German riots in Prague, was arrested and was forced to leave his grammar school. He trained as a druggist and then graduated from the Czech-Slavonic Business Academy. In 1903, with Ladislav Hájek, he wrote a parody of lyrical poetry, his first humorous work. He was dismissed from the Slavia Bank on 28 May 1903 for absence, and then lived by journalism and writing, in a bohemian way.

In 1907 Hašek edited the anarchist magazine Komuna and was briefly imprisoned. In 1909 he had sixty-four short stories published, and he became editor of Svět zvířat, a magazine on animals, until he was dismissed in October 1910, reportedly after writing articles about non-existent animals. In 1911 he founded with friends the Party of Moderate Progress Within the Bounds of the Law, a parody of political life. He also co-wrote cabaret performances with František Langer, Emil Artur Longen and Egon Erwin Kisch.

He was called up in February 1915 into the Austro-Hungarian 91st Infantry Regiment and was captured by the Russians on 24 September 1915. He joined the Czechoslovak Legion in 1916 and fought at the Battle of Zborov. In 1918 he left the Legion for Moscow and the Red Army, and served in Samara, Ufa and Siberia, where he published several magazines. He returned to Prague in December 1920.

Back in Czechoslovakia, where the Soviets had sent him to organise the communist movement, he was prevented by circumstances and returned to a bohemian life in the pubs of Prague. On 25 August 1921 he moved to Lipnice nad Sázavou, seriously ill, and began The Fateful Adventures of the Good Soldier Švejk During the World War. When he could no longer write, he dictated chapters from his bedroom. He died of heart disease on 3 January 1923, and the novel was left unfinished. It satirises the ineptitude of authority figures and is the most translated novel in Czech literature, in about 60 languages. Josef Lada, with whom Hašek lived at the outbreak of the First World War, later illustrated it.
jaswant-singh-of-marwar: Jaswant Singh was born on 26 December 1626 at Burhanpur, the youngest son of Maharaja Gaj Singh of Marwar. He succeeded on 6 May 1638 by special decree of Emperor Shah Jahan and was installed at Mehrangarh in Jodhpur on 25 May 1638. His father's favourite concubine, Anara Begum, who regarded him as her own son and was at odds with the heir apparent Amar Singh Rathore, had a part in his accession; Amar Singh was later given Nagore in compensation. He held in jagir the parganas of Jodhpur, Siwana, Merta, Sojat, Phalodi and Pokharan, and Shah Jahan granted him the personal title of Maharaja on 6 January 1654.

Shah Jahan sent him to stop the advance of the rebel princes Aurangzeb and Murad. The armies met at Dharmatpur, fifteen miles from Ujjain, on 15 April 1658. His advisers proposed a night raid on Aurangzeb's artillery and gunpowder, since the Rajput army was almost wholly light cavalry; he is quoted as answering that it was inconsistent with the manliness of the Rajputs to employ stratagems or make a night attack. He was defeated and lost 6,000 men, among them Ratan Singh Rathore of Ratlam and Mokand Das Hada of Kota.

Posted to the Deccan, he made Pune his headquarters. In 1664 he besieged Kondana without success, and he left for Delhi after Jai Singh was sent to the Deccan. He returned in 1667 with Prince Muazzam, the new viceroy, and acted as an intermediary between Shivaji and Aurangzeb. In 1670 he was posted at Burhanpur.

His son Prithviraj Singh died at Delhi on 8 May 1667; the khyats, the chronicles of Marwar, say that Aurangzeb had given him a poisoned robe. Jaswant Singh died at Jamrud, near Peshawar, on a date usually converted as 28 December 1678, though another scholar makes it 28 November 1678. Two of his wives were pregnant at his death and both bore sons, which led to a war over the installation of Ajit Singh Rathore as ruler of Marwar. He was also a man of letters, the author of the Siddhant-Bodh, the Anand Vilas and the Bhasha-Bhushan.
jataka-tales: The word jātaka means of the birth. According to the traditional account in the Pali Jātakanidāna, a prologue to the stories, Gautama vowed in front of a past Buddha, Dipankara, to become a Buddha himself, and then spent many lifetimes on the path. The stories from those lives are recorded as jātakas. The genre rests on the idea that the Buddha could recall all his past lives and used the memories to illustrate his teachings.

The tales may be very old. Depictions in early Indian art go back as far as the second century BCE, and many narratives survive in almost identical form in the canons of different schools, which suggests that they date from before the schisms between those schools. Sarah Shaw dates the verse portions of the Pali Jātaka to the fifth century BCE and says later parts were added up to the third century CE.

In these stories the future Buddha may appear as a king, an outcaste, a deva or an animal, and whatever his form he shows a virtue that the tale teaches. Many follow a threefold plan: a narrative in the present, a story from a past life, and a link in which the characters of the past are identified with those of the present. The tales illustrate the perfections of a bodhisattva, such as generosity, and teach moral lessons within the framework of karma and rebirth.

The largest known collection is the Jātakatthavaṇṇanā of the Theravada school, part of the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Pali Canon, which holds 547 jātakas in verse and prose and was collected around 500 CE. Other sources include the Cariyāpiṭaka, which includes 35 jātakas, and Āryaśūra's Sanskrit Jātakamālā.

Jātakas were among the first texts translated into Chinese, and Kāng Sēnghuì, working at Nanking around 247, was one of their first translators. The earliest known illustrations are on the railings of the Bharhut stupa and at Sanchi, from the late second to the first century BCE, and they later appear at Ajanta and at Bagan, where the Ananda Temple depicts 554 tales. The Chinese pilgrim Yijing said that jātaka plays were performed throughout the five countries of India in the 7th century.

The Vessantara Jataka is still recited and performed in Theravada countries. E. B. Cowell and others translated the Pali collection into English in six volumes between 1895 and 1907. A jātaka was also adapted by the 10th-century Shia scholar Ibn Bābūya as Balawhar wa-Būdāsf, which became the Christian story of Barlaam and Joasaph.
jats: The Jats, also spelt Jaats and Jatts, were originally nomadic pastoralists in the lower Indus River Valley of Sindh and Makran, and they gradually became farmers. Many moved north into the Punjab and then into Delhi, north-eastern Rajasthan and the western Gangetic Plain at the turn of the second millennium CE. The word Jat comes from the Prakrit Jaṭṭa, itself from Jarta or Jartika, the name of an ancient non-Vedic Bahlika tribe. The first mention of Jats is in an inscription from Gilgit-Baltistan dated to the 6th or 7th century. From the Mughal era in Punjab, Jat was used more as a socioeconomic status than an ethnic label, and the Jats were often associated with the peasantry.

Before they settled in the Punjab and other northern regions, the pastoralist Jats had little exposure to the mainstream religions, according to the historians Catherine Asher and Cynthia Talbot, and they adopted the dominant religion of the people among whom they lived. Several clans have traditions of converting to Islam in the first half of the second millennium CE under the influence of Sufi saints, and by the 16th century many Punjabi clans west of the Ravi River were Muslim. Jats moved onto the Gangetic Plain in two large migrations, in the 17th and 18th centuries, as an umbrella group of peasant-warriors rather than a caste in the usual Hindu sense.

Significant conversions of Jats to Sikhism occurred as early as the time of Guru Angad, but the first large-scale conversions are commonly held to have begun under Guru Arjan, who founded towns such as Tarn Taran Sahib, Kartarpur and Hargobindpur. The Jats formed the vanguard of Sikh resistance against the Mughal Empire from the 18th century onwards. At the partition of India many Muslim Jats migrated to Pakistan, while some stayed in India as Muley Jats. By the 20th century landowning Jats had become an influential group in Punjab, western Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi.

Jat marriage is traditionally structured around clan (gotra) exogamy and village exogamy, while Jats marry within their own community. The Khap system, councils of clan elders and notables, was historically the prevailing form of organisation, and it continues today as an extrajudicial body without legal recognition. Scholars disagree on the varna status of the Jats in Hinduism: the historian Irfan Habib cites a Shudra status in the 11th century that had become Vaishya by the 17th. The Arya Samaj, popular among them, advanced a claim to Kshatriya status.
java: Java is one of the Greater Sunda Islands, lying between Sumatra to the west and Bali to the east, with the Java Sea to the north and the Indian Ocean to the south. It is almost entirely of volcanic origin, and a chain of volcanic mountains forms the east–west spine of the island and splits the interior into relatively isolated regions suited to wet-rice cultivation. Indonesian coffee was first grown there from 1699. Fossils of Homo erectus, known as Java Man and dated to 1.3 million years ago, were found on the banks of the Bengawan Solo River.

Wet-field rice cultivation required cooperation between villages, and out of these alliances small kingdoms developed. The period from the 5th to the 15th century is called the Hindu-Buddhist or Classic period. The Taruma kingdom of western Java existed from the 5th to the 7th centuries, and the first state to leave a substantial record was the Mataram kingdom, founded in central Java at the beginning of the 8th century. Its rulers patronised both Hindu and Buddhist institutions. From the second half of the 8th century they called themselves members of the Sailendra dynasty, and Borobudur was built in the late 8th century and Prambanan in the mid-9th.

Islam became the dominant religion through the 16th century, first in the north-coast port cities such as Surabaya, Gresik, Demak and Cirebon, through contact with foreign Muslim traders. Demak was the first Muslim kingdom to achieve a degree of hegemony and defeated the remnants of the Majapahit kingdom. At the turn of the 17th century the inland kingdom of Mataram became dominant in central and eastern Java, and under Sultan Agung, who reigned from 1613 to 1646, it subjugated the coastal principalities of Surabaya and Cirebon.

Contact with European powers began in 1522 with a treaty between the Sunda kingdom and the Portuguese in Malacca. A Dutch expedition under Cornelis de Houtman made the first Dutch contact in 1596. By the end of the 18th century the Dutch East India Company had extended its influence over the interior sultanates, intervening in wars between rival Mataram claimants. In the 1750s Sultan Mangkubumi tried to restore Mataram's control, but the Dutch divided the kingdom into the Surakarta and Yogyakarta principalities. Indonesian nationalism took hold in the early 20th century, and independence was recognised in 1949.

Java is part of Indonesia and the world's most populous island, home to about 56 percent of the country's people. Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia, lies on its north-western coast. The main languages are Javanese, Sundanese, Madurese and Betawi. Five of Indonesia's World Heritage Sites are on the island, among them Borobudur and Prambanan.
java-sea: The Java Sea lies on the Sunda Shelf, between Borneo to the north, Java to the south, Sumatra to the west and Sulawesi to the east. The Karimata Strait on its north-western side links it to the South China Sea. It is generally considered part of the western Pacific Ocean, though it is occasionally counted as part of the Indian Ocean. The sea covers the southern section of the Sunda Shelf, with a surface area of about 320,000 square kilometres. It measures about 1,600 kilometres from east to west and 380 kilometres from north to south, and its mean depth is only 46 metres.

The sea formed as sea levels rose at the end of the last ice age. Its almost uniformly flat bottom, and drainage channels that can be traced to the mouths of island rivers, show that the Sunda Shelf was once a stable, dry land of low relief. A few granite hills that resisted erosion were left standing above it and are now the islands.

From February to March 1942 the Battle of the Java Sea was fought here, one of the costliest naval battles of the World War II. The naval forces of the Netherlands, Britain, Australia and the United States were nearly destroyed in trying to defend Java from Japanese attack.

The seafloor of the southern part is geologically similar to northern Java, where oil fields occur and extend under the sea, and the exploration of petroleum and natural gas here has become the basis of Indonesia's national export programme. Fishing is an important activity, and more than 3,000 species of marine life are found in the area. Karimunjawa is one of several national parks, and the Thousand Islands lie north of Jakarta, forming the city's only regency.
javier-perez-de-cuellar: Javier Pérez de Cuéllar was born on 19 January 1920 in Lima, to a rentier family of Spanish descent whose ancestors had migrated from Spain in the sixteenth century. His father died when he was four. He attended the Colegio San Agustín, learned French from a governess and took a law degree at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru in 1943. He joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1940 as an intern and the diplomatic service in 1944, serving first at Peru's embassy in France, where he married Yvette Roberts-Darricau in 1947.

He was a member of the Peruvian delegation to the first session of the United Nations General Assembly in London in 1946, and later served as ambassador to Switzerland, the Soviet Union and Poland, and Venezuela.

In 1971 he became Peru's permanent representative to the United Nations. He sat on the Security Council in 1973 and 1974, presiding when the Cypriot coup took place in July 1974, and from 1975 to 1977 he was the Secretary-General's Special Representative in Cyprus. In 1979 he became under-secretary-general for Special Political Affairs and in 1981 the Secretary-General's personal representative on Afghanistan. In December 1981 he was selected to succeed Kurt Waldheim as Secretary-General, and he was re-elected unanimously in October 1986.

As Secretary-General he mediated between the United Kingdom and Argentina after the Falklands War, supported the Contadora group in Central America and in 1983 initiated the World Commission on Environment and Development. He worked on Namibian independence, Western Sahara, Cyprus, the Iran–Iraq War and the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan, and in March 1986 formally accused Iraq of using chemical weapons against Iran. His second term ended on 31 December 1991, after Boutros Boutros-Ghali was agreed as successor in November.

Pérez de Cuéllar ran unsuccessfully against Alberto Fujimori for the presidency of Peru in 1995 and was prime minister and foreign minister from November 2000 to July 2001. He then served as ambassador to France until 2004. In 1997 he published a memoir of his United Nations years, Pilgrimage for Peace. He received the Prince of Asturias Award for International Cooperation in 1987 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1991. He died at his home in Lima on 4 March 2020, two months after his hundredth birthday, the first secretary-general of the United Nations to become a centenarian.
jawaharlal-nehru: Jawaharlal Nehru was born on 14 November 1889 in Allahabad to Swarup Rani and Motilal Nehru, a wealthy, self-made barrister who served as president of the Indian National Congress in 1919 and 1928. Both parents were Kashmiri Pandits. Nehru grew up in the mansion Anand Bhavan and was educated at home by governesses and tutors. He became an ardent nationalist in his youth, stirred by the Second Boer War and the Russo-Japanese War.

He was educated at Harrow School and Trinity College, Cambridge, from which he graduated in 1910 with an honours degree in natural science, and trained in the law at the Inner Temple. After returning to India in August 1912 he enrolled at the Allahabad High Court, but had little interest in the law, and nationalist politics gradually replaced his practice.

Nehru met Mahatma Gandhi in 1916.
