The Thirty Years' War damaged the town several times, and between 1622 and 1684 it stood at the centre of the Northern Moravia witch trials. A fire in 1696 caused severe damage. In 1742, after the First Silesian War, it became part of Austrian Silesia and lost its Silesian markets, so that the linen trade fell into crisis. Industrialisation brought new factories in the 19th century, among them a textile works founded in 1822, and a railway opened in 1888. In 1938 the Munich Agreement ceded the town to Nazi Germany, and in 1945 it returned to Czechoslovakia and its German population was expelled.

Jeseník has about 10,000 inhabitants and is known for the Priessnitz Medical Spa, founded by Vincenz Priessnitz in 1822 as the world's first hydrotherapy institute; his birth house is now a museum, and his tomb dates from 1853. The Gräfenberg hamlet, founded in 1808, was incorporated into the town in 1868. The oldest monument is the Jeseník Water Fortress, a Gothic castle of the 13th century first documented in 1374, which houses the regional museum. The town hall dates from 1710.
jesuits: Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque nobleman of Spanish origin with a military background, discerned his vocation while recovering from a wound received at the Battle of Pamplona. On 15 August 1534 he and six companions, students at the University of Paris, met in a crypt at Montmartre to promise poverty, chastity and obedience. They were Francis Xavier, Alfonso Salmerón, Diego Laínez, Nicolás Bobadilla, Peter Faber and Simão Rodrigues. The society was founded in 1540 with the approval of Pope Paul III.

The Jesuits arose just before the Council of Trent and the Counter-Reformation, but Ignatius and the early Jesuits recognised that the hierarchical church needed reform. They struggled against corruption and spiritual lassitude, and Ignatius insisted on a high level of academic preparation for the clergy. A Jesuit professes perpetual poverty, chastity and obedience and promises special obedience to the pope regarding missions. The order is led for life by a superior general.

Jesuit missionaries established missions around the world from the 16th to the 18th century, with successes and failures. In Japan the government granted them the fiefdom of Nagasaki in 1580 and removed it in 1587 out of fear of their growing influence. In Latin America their ascendancy grew in the 17th century, with new missions in Peru, Colombia and Bolivia, and by 1603 there were 345 Jesuit priests in Mexico alone. In some places they protected indigenous peoples from slavers, notably the Guaraní, but elsewhere they enslaved indigenous people after wars in which resistance to European colonisation was defeated.

The Jesuits were always controversial and often clashed with governments. They were banished from France in 1594 after Jean Châtel, who had studied at their Collège de Clermont, tried to kill Henri IV, though the ban was soon lifted. The Jesuit scholar Andrew Dial calculated that the order owned more than 20,000 slaves worldwide in 1760, mostly in the Americas, and Jesuits also took part in the Atlantic slave trade. From 1759 the Church expelled them from most of Europe and its colonies, and on 21 July 1773 Pope Clement XIV suppressed the order. The suppression was lifted in 1814.

Jesuit spirituality draws on the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius, which aim to find God in all things, and on the Examen, a daily review of the day's events. Formation for the priesthood takes eight to fourteen years. The Decree de genere of 1593 barred anyone of Jewish or Muslim ancestry, contrary to Ignatius's own wishes, and was repealed only in 1946. Jesuit schools, whose studies followed Aristotle under the Ratio Studiorum of 1599, were joined by scientific work in fields from cosmology to seismology, and the order has been described as the most important contributor to experimental physics in the seventeenth century.
jesus: A Jewish person in the time of Jesus usually had only one name, sometimes followed by a patronymic or a home town, and so Jesus is commonly called Jesus of Nazareth in the New Testament. His name is the English transliteration, through Latin Iesus, of the Greek rendering of the Hebrew Yehoshua, shortened by that period to Yeshua; it means God saves. The word Christ is a title, not a given name, from the Greek Christos, meaning anointed, a calque of the Hebrew mashiakh, or messiah.

According to Christian tradition as represented in the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, Jesus was circumcised at eight days old and presented at the Temple in Jerusalem at 40 days. He was baptized by John the Baptist as a young adult. After 40 days and nights of fasting in the Judean wilderness he began his public ministry.

The four canonical gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, are the foremost sources for his life and message. By the usual scholarly view, Mark was written first, and Matthew and Luke used it as a source.

According to the New Testament accounts, Jesus was an itinerant teacher whom his followers believed to possess divine authority in interpreting Jewish law. He debated with other Jews, most commonly the Pharisees and Sadducees, engaged in healings, taught in parables, and gathered followers, 12 of whom he appointed as his apostles. He was arrested in Jerusalem, tried by the Sanhedrin, and handed over to the Roman authorities, and was crucified on the order of Pontius Pilate.

Christians hold that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day after his death, a belief that became the foundation of the early Christian Church. His first followers were Jews, and the first Christian community was centred in Jerusalem, with Peter, James the brother of Jesus, and John the Apostle among its leaders. After his conversion Paul the Apostle spread his teachings to non-Jewish communities in the eastern Mediterranean. By the end of the 1st century Christianity began to be recognised as a separate religion from Judaism.

Scholars have pursued three quests for the historical Jesus since the 18th century. They agree that he existed, though their portraits differ from each other and from the gospels. Mainstream Judaism rejects the belief that he was the awaited messiah. In Islam he is considered the messiah and a prophet of God, and most Muslims do not believe he was crucified.
jet-engine: Before the Second World War, engineers were beginning to realise that engines driving propellers were approaching performance limits, because propeller efficiency declined as the blade tips approached the speed of sound. A different means of propulsion was needed to raise aircraft performance further, and this motivated the development of the gas turbine, the most common form of jet engine. Its key feature is that the turbine extracts power from the engine itself to drive the compressor.

The gas turbine was not a new idea. John Barber was granted a patent for a stationary turbine in England in 1791, and the Norwegian engineer Ægidius Elling built the first gas turbine to run self-sustaining in 1903. Such engines did not reach manufacture because of problems of safety, reliability, weight and above all sustained operation. Maxime Guillaume's patent of 1921 described an axial-flow turbojet that would have needed considerable advances in compressors. Alan Arnold Griffith published An Aerodynamic Theory of Turbine Design in 1926, which led to experimental work at the RAE.

A jet engine discharges a fast-moving jet of heated gas, usually air, and generates thrust by jet propulsion. The term usually means an internal combustion air-breathing engine such as a turbojet, turbofan, ramjet, pulse jet or scramjet, although the broad definition can include rocket, water jet and hybrid propulsion. A turbojet compresses air, mixes fuel with it, burns the mixture in a combustor and passes the hot, high-pressure gas through a turbine, which drives the compressor, and then a nozzle. The turbofan adds a fan at the front that accelerates air through a duct around the core, and it is the dominant type for medium and long-range airliners.

A rocket engine uses the same basic principle of thrust but carries all its reaction mass, so it can work at any altitude and in space. Ramjets and scramjets use the ram effect of the vehicle's speed instead of a mechanical compressor, and turboshaft and turboprop engines share components with jet engines.

Early jet aircraft used turbojets, which were relatively inefficient for subsonic flight, and most modern subsonic jet aircraft use high-bypass turbofans, which give higher speed and better fuel efficiency than piston and propeller engines over long distances. The thrust of a typical jetliner engine rose from 5,000 lbf in the de Havilland Ghost turbojet of the 1950s to 115,000 lbf in the General Electric GE90 turbofan of the 1990s, while in-flight shutdowns fell from 40 to fewer than 1 per 100,000 engine flight hours. This allowed routine transatlantic flights by twin-engined airliners.

Jet engines also power cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles. Designs derived from military turbojets such as the Pratt & Whitney J57 and J75 serve as industrial gas turbines for generating electricity, driving pumps and propelling ships and locomotives.
jever: Jever is the capital of the district of Friesland in Lower Saxony. It lies in Jeverland, in the north-eastern part of the East Frisian peninsula near the North Sea coast, about 15 kilometres west of Wilhelmshaven. The town stands on a flat tongue of the Oldenburg–East Frisian geest, which rises 7 to 8 metres above the surrounding marshes. Several tiefs, watercourses close to the sea that drain the land behind the dikes, surround it. Archaeological finds show that the area has been inhabited since the Neolithic: a dolmen stood near the town until at least 1880, and flint tools, urns, a bronze spear tip and a socket axe have been found.

Jever was granted city status in 1536, and the ring of moats and earthen walls called the Gräfte was built that year to protect it. Three wooden gates with bridges gave access. At the start of the 19th century the earth walls were removed and the canals filled where the gates had stood, leaving the Graften that still surround the historic centre. The town is sometimes called Marienstadt after Maria of Jever (1500–1575), the last independent ruler of the Lordship of Jever, who ruled from 1517. From 1560 to 1564 she had the castle altered in Renaissance style.

Jever Castle grew from a fortified complex of the 14th century and was the seat of the lordship, with a mighty Bergfried at its centre that was integrated from the 16th century into a four-wing complex with moats and ramparts. Under Prince Friedrich August of Anhalt-Zerbst, a well decree of 9 October 1756 made each public fountain the charge of a named group of residents, the Püttacht, a custom the Püttbierfest still recalls each January. In 1825 the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss stayed in Jever for survey work, and the town served as a triangulation station.

Jever is known for its castle, which has housed the Castle Museum of cultural history since 1921, and for its brewery, the maker of Jever Pilsener, with a historical brewery museum. The Evangelical Lutheran town church, consecrated in 1736, burned down on 1 October 1959. Natives include the agricultural economist Johann Heinrich von Thünen (1783–1850) and the historian Friedrich Christoph Schlosser (1776–1861), and the psychiatrist and philosopher Karl Jaspers (1883–1969) often visited his grandparents there.
jezebel: Jezebel is introduced in the Book of Kings as a Phoenician princess, the daughter of a king of Tyre. The first Book of Kings, chapter 16, calls her Sidonian, a biblical term for Phoenicians in general. She married King Ahab of Samaria, in the northern kingdom of Israel. Israel Finkelstein calls the marriage a brilliant stroke of international diplomacy that showed the power and prestige of Ahab and his kingdom. The name is an Anglicized form of the Hebrew ʾIzeḇel, often interpreted as Where is the Lord?, a ritual cry in worship of Baal. Ahab built a Baalist altar in a house of Baal in Samaria.

As queen, Jezebel according to the Hebrew Bible institutionalised Baal worship, killed Yahwist prophets and desecrated their altars. The prophet Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal and Asherah to a contest at Mount Carmel to see which god would burn a bull sacrifice. Her prophets failed, and Elijah then ordered the people to seize and kill them. Jezebel vowed to kill Elijah, who fled to Mount Horeb. In the account of Naboth she resolved a failed deal between Ahab and Naboth over a vineyard by ordering the execution of Naboth and his sons on false charges of blasphemy. Elijah condemned this and foretold doom for her family.

After Ahab's death in battle their son Ahaziah inherited the throne, and his brother Jehoram succeeded him. Jehu usurped the throne and killed Jehoram. When he came to Jezreel, Jezebel put on make-up and a wig and looked out of a window to taunt him. Geoffrey Bromiley reads this as the defiance of a queen mother. Jehu had her eunuch servants throw her from the window, and only her skull, feet and palms were left of her body, as Elijah had prophesied.

Scholars disagree about the historicity of the story. Finkelstein considers it more of a historical novel than a chronicle, shaped by the theology of 7th-century BCE writers, while Brian R. Doak argues for its plausibility. A 9th-century BCE seal inscribed YZBL may once have read as belonging to Jezebel, but scholars do not agree. The name later came to stand for false prophets and then for fallen or promiscuous women.
jharkhand: Jharkhand is a landlocked state of eastern India, bordered by West Bengal to the east, Chhattisgarh to the west, Uttar Pradesh to the north-west, Bihar to the north and Odisha to the south. Its name means 'the land of forests', from jhar, 'forest', and khand, 'land'. It covers 79,716 square kilometres, much of it on the Chota Nagpur Plateau, crossed by the Damodar, North Koel, Barakar, South Koel, Sankh and Subarnarekha rivers. Forests still cover much of the state and sustain elephants and tigers. The Parasnath Hill in Giridih district, 1,365 metres high, is the chief Jain pilgrimage site and is called Marang Buru by the Santal, whose supreme deity it names.

The region has been inhabited since the Mesolithic and Chalcolithic periods, as cave paintings at Isko in Hazaribagh district, dated to between 9000 and 5000 BCE, show. In the second millennium BCE copper tools spread across the Chota Nagpur Plateau in what is known as the Copper Hoard Culture, and iron slag from Singhbhum district has been dated by carbon to 1400 BCE. The Nanda, Maurya and Gupta empires ruled the region in ancient times. The Chinese traveller Xuanzang passed through it in the seventh century and described the kingdom of Karnasuvarna under Shashanka. In the medieval period the Nagvanshi, Pala, Khayaravala, Ramgarh Raj and Chero rulers governed it.

Mughal influence reached Palamu when the Rajput Raja Mansingh conquered it in 1574 under Emperor Akbar. A separate tribal state was demanded in 1928, when Unnati Samaj, the political wing of the Christian Tribals Association, submitted a memorandum to the Simon Commission. In 1955 the Jharkhand Party, led by Jaipal Singh Munda, asked the States Reorganization Commission for a state of the tribal area of south Bihar, which was rejected. Jharkhand was finally carved out of the southern part of Bihar in 2000, with 18 districts that were formerly part of south Bihar.

Hindi is the official language, and Ranchi is the capital with Dumka as sub-capital. The census of 2011 counted 32.96 million people, of whom 26.21 percent belong to Scheduled Tribes. Besides Hindi, speakers of Indo-Aryan, Dravidian and Austroasiatic languages live in the state, and sixteen further languages, among them Santali, Mundari, Ho, Kurukh and Nagpuri, have additional official status. Hinduism is the largest religion, with 67.8 percent, and Sarnaism, a tribal faith, is the second largest of its kinds, with 12.5 percent. The state has large reserves of iron ore, coal, copper ore, mica, bauxite and uranium.
jiang-qing: Jiang Qing was born in Zhucheng, Shandong, in March 1914. Her father, Li Dewen, was a carpenter, and her mother was his subsidiary wife. He abused her mother almost every day, and after he broke her finger one Lantern Festival the mother fled with the child and found work as a domestic servant. At 14 Jiang joined a local underground theatre troupe and then trained at the Experimental Arts Academy in Jinan. In Shanghai she joined the Communist Youth League and returned to the stage. She joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1933.

Jiang went to Yan'an, where in 1938 she became a drama instructor at the new Lu Xun Academy of Arts, and she married Mao Zedong that year. After the People's Republic was founded in 1949 she wielded considerable influence over the arts. She organised campaigns against the film The Life of Wu Xun and the Peking opera Hai Rui Dismissed from Office and promoted revolutionary operas known as yangbanxi. From 1962 she appeared in public as Mao's wife and gave speeches in the cultural and propaganda sectors, condemning various figures.

By late 1965 she had gathered allies such as Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan, and her campaign against Hai Rui Dismissed from Office marked the start of the Cultural Revolution. She became a major figure from 1966 to 1976, a Politburo member at the Ninth and Tenth Central Committees and the de facto leader of the Cultural Revolution Group. She also used the movement against personal enemies, among them people who had slighted her during her acting career in the 1930s. With Zhang, Yao and Wang Hongwen she formed the group Mao called the Gang of Four.

In the mid-1970s Jiang led the campaign against Deng Xiaoping. When Mao lay critically ill in September 1976 she proposed expelling Deng at a Politburo meeting but did not succeed, and after Mao's death she was arrested and expelled from the party. The indictment against the Gang of Four had 48 counts. In the televised trial she was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve, and in 1983 the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. She was held at Qincheng Prison.

According to Ross Terrill's biography, she died by suicide in a Beijing hospital on 14 May 1991, a claim disputed by a former Qincheng official who said she died in prison. The Chinese public blamed her for the upheavals of the Cultural Revolution.
jiang-zemin: Jiang Zemin was born in Yangzhou, Jiangsu, on 17 August 1926 and grew up during the Japanese occupation. His uncle and foster father, Jiang Shangqing, died fighting the Japanese and was regarded as a national hero, and Jiang became his male heir. He studied electrical engineering at the National Central University, joined the Chinese Communist Party while in college, and graduated from the National Chiao Tung University in 1947. In the 1950s he trained at the Stalin Automobile Works in Moscow. From 1970 to 1972 he led an expert team that set up fifteen machinery plants in Romania. He became a member of the Central Committee in 1982.

Jiang became mayor of Shanghai in 1985, and in 1987 its party secretary and a member of the Politburo. After the Tiananmen Square protests and massacre of 1989 he unexpectedly replaced Zhao Ziyang as general secretary, as a compromise candidate, appointed on 24 June 1989 with a small power base. He also took over the chairmanship of the Central Military Commission from Deng Xiaoping, and he became president in 1993. After Deng's southern tour of 1992 he introduced the term socialist market economy, and his administration oversaw the breaking of the iron rice bowl and the privatization of many state-owned enterprises. He forbade the military to engage in business. In 1999 he began a crackdown on Falun Gong.

Hong Kong returned from the United Kingdom in 1997 and Macau from Portugal in 1999, and China entered the World Trade Organization in 2001. Relations with the United States were marked by tensions, including the Third Taiwan Strait Crisis of 1996. On 25 February 2000 he introduced the theory of the Three Represents, which justified admitting private business owners to the party and was written into its constitution in 2002.

Jiang gave up his leadership posts between 2002 and 2005, handing them to Hu Jintao, though he and his faction kept an influence on affairs for some time. He died in Shanghai on 30 November 2022, at 96, and was given a state funeral. In China his reputation is mixed: some credit his term with the relative stability and growth of the 1990s, while others argue that he did little to correct the imbalances built up by years of fast economic reform.
jiangsu: Jiangsu is a coastal province of East China, bordering Shandong to the north, Anhui to the west, and Zhejiang and Shanghai to the south. It has a coastline of over 1,000 kilometres along the Yellow Sea. The land is flat: plains cover 68 percent of the province, and most of it stands no more than 50 metres above sea level. The well-developed irrigation system earned the south the name shuixiang, land of water, and Suzhou has so many canals that it has been called the Venice of the East. The Grand Canal crosses the province from north to south, and the Yangtze flows through its southern part.

In the earliest Chinese dynasties the area lay far from the centre of Chinese civilisation and was home to the Huai people. Under the Zhou the state of Wu appeared in southern Jiangsu. Near the end of the Spring and Autumn period it became a great power under King Helu and in 484 BCE defeated Qi, but in 473 BCE it was conquered by the state of Yue. Yue was in turn subjugated by Chu in 333 BCE, and Qin unified China in 221 BCE. Since the Sui and Tang dynasties Jiangsu has been a national economic and commercial centre, partly because of the Grand Canal.

The name combines the first elements of two cities, Jiangning, now Nanjing, and Suzhou. In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek established a government at Nanjing, and Shanghai separated from Jiangsu in 1927. Nanjing fell to the Japanese on 13 December 1937, and the atrocities of the following three months became known as the Rape of Nanjing. It then became the seat of the collaborationist government of East China under Wang Jingwei, and most of Jiangsu stayed under Japanese occupation until 1945.

Jiangsu is a province of the People's Republic of China with its capital at Nanjing and a population of about 85 million, the most densely populated of the country's provinces. It is divided into thirteen prefecture-level cities, among them Nanjing, Suzhou, Wuxi, Changzhou and Zhenjiang. Most residents are ethnic Han Chinese, with Hui and Manchu minorities. The southern part, centred on the Shanghai-Nanjing corridor, is the more urban and prosperous, while the north is more rural.
jiangxi: Jiangxi lies on the banks of the Yangtze in the north and rises into hillier country in the south and east. Mountains surround it on three sides, and the highest point is Mount Huanggang in the Wuyi Mountains, at 2,157 metres. The Gan River flows through the whole province from south to north into Lake Poyang, the largest freshwater lake in China, which empties into the Yangtze. The Gan valley was historically the main north-south transport route of south China, one of the few easy corridors through the rugged south-eastern mountains. It carried trade between the North China Plain and the Yangtze valley and the territory of modern Guangdong, so the region was strategically important throughout much of Chinese history.

Jiangxi lay outside the sphere of early Chinese civilisation under the Shang, and peoples collectively known as the Baiyue probably lived there. Its north formed the western frontier of the state of Wu, and after Yue conquered Wu in 473 BCE, Chu took northern Jiangxi. Yuzhang Commandery, established at the start of the Han dynasty, was the first commandery set up there by a Chinese dynasty. It took its name from the original name of the Gan River, and Gan is now the province's abbreviation. In 291 it became its own zhou, Jiangzhou, under the Western Jin. In 733 the Tang divided the Jiangnan Circuit, and the western half, the Jiangnanxi Circuit, gave the province its modern name.

After the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, Jiangxi Province was established for the first time, and it took roughly its modern borders. After the fall of the Qing it became one of the earliest Communist bases. The Nanchang Uprising took place there on 1 August 1927. The government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was established at Ruijin in 1931, and in 1935, encircled by Nationalist forces, the Communists broke through and began the Long March to Yan'an. The brutal campaigns and purges of those years reduced the population by 40 per cent, to 13.8 million in 1936.

Nanchang is the provincial capital, and Ganzhou and Jiujiang are other major cities. Most of the population is Han Chinese, and the province is the centre of Gan Chinese, with some Hakka also spoken. It has deposits of copper, tungsten, gold, silver, uranium and lithium. After the opening of the Yuehan Railway in 1936 and of the Zhegan Railway in 1937, Jiujiang's port declined in importance. The province was fully under Communist control from the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
jigawa-state: Jigawa State lies in the north-west of Nigeria, between latitudes 11°N and 13°N, and covers about 22,410 square kilometres. It borders Kano and Katsina states to the west, Bauchi State to the east and Yobe State to the north-east, and along its northern edge it shares a 70 km international border with the Zinder Region of Niger. Its land is undulating, with sand dunes spanning several kilometres in places. The main rivers are the Hadejia, Kafin Hausa and Iggi, and the Hadejia–Kafin Hausa river crosses the state from west to east through the Hadejia-Nguru wetlands into the Lake Chad Basin. Most of the state lies within the Sudan savannah.

The state is known for the Dutsen Habude cave paintings at Birnin Kudu, which have been dated to the Neolithic period. The town of Hadejia, formerly Biram, is notable as one of the traditional seven true Hausa states. The area was formerly the north-eastern part of Kano State. Agitation for a separate state was led by Malam Inuwa-Dutse, a former commissioner in the ministry of agriculture and natural resources under Audu Bako, governor of the old Kano State. Jigawa was created on 27 August 1991 under the military administration of General Ibrahim Babangida.

The capital and largest city is Dutse, and the state has twenty-seven local government areas. The people are predominantly Hausa and Fulani, with Kanuri mainly in the Hadejia Emirate, and Islam and a long history of intermarriage bind the three groups together. The state is governed under Sharia law. Over 80% of the population is engaged in subsistence farming and animal husbandry, and trade is mostly small and medium in scale. The state has universities at Dutse, Babura, Kafin Hausa and Majia, and a federal polytechnic at Kazaure.
jihlava: Jihlava began as a Slavic market village on a trade route around 1200 and is first mentioned in 1233. Silver mining began in 1234, and the royal mining town was established between 1233 and 1240, making it the oldest mining town in what is now the Czech Republic. It was the first city in central Europe where mining law was codified. Miners came from Bavaria, Saxony and other German-speaking lands, and King Ottokar II's building regulations of 1270 set its rectangular plan around a large square.

By the end of the 14th century the richest deposits were exhausted and Jihlava turned to trade and cloth making. During the Hussite Wars it stayed a Catholic stronghold, and on 5 July 1436 a treaty was made there in which the Hussites acknowledged Sigismund as king of Bohemia. A fire in 1523 badly damaged the town, and Swedish troops captured it twice in the Thirty Years' War.

In the second half of the 18th century Jihlava was the second largest cloth producer in the Austrian Empire. In 1921 about 54 per cent of its people were German speakers, and it formed the centre of a German-speaking enclave. The synagogue was burnt in 1939, and most of the town's Jewish population, over 1,000 people, was deported and killed. After the Second World War most German speakers were expelled under the Beneš decrees.

Jihlava is the capital of the Vysočina Region, on the historic border of Moravia and Bohemia, about 110 kilometres south-east of Prague, with about 54,000 inhabitants. Its historic centre, a mixture of Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings, is protected as an urban monument reservation, and the early Gothic Church of Saint James the Great is a national cultural monument. Gustav Mahler lived there from 1860 to 1875, and his parents lie in the Jewish cemetery.
jilin: In ancient times the Jilin area was inhabited by the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and Wùjí, and the kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo ruled parts of it. The region then fell successively under the Xiongnu, the Xianbei state, Goguryeo, Balhae, the Khitan Liao dynasty, the Jurchen Jin dynasty and the Mongol Yuan dynasty. Under the Qing, much of the area was controlled by the General of Jilin, whose territory extended to much of what is now Russia's Primorsky Krai.

After Primorsky Krai was ceded to Russia in 1860, the government began to open the area to Han Chinese migrants, most of them from Shandong, and by the early 20th century the Han had become the dominant ethnic group of the region. In 1932 the area was incorporated into Manchukuo, a puppet state set up by Japan, with Changchun, then called Xinjing, as its capital. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the Red Army captured Jilin in Operation August Storm, and the region, with the rest of north-eastern China, passed to the Communists. Manchuria was the staging ground from which they conquered the rest of China in the Chinese Civil War.

In 1949 the province was smaller, taking in only the environs of Changchun and Jilin City, with its capital at Jilin City, while Changchun was an independent municipality. It was expanded to its present borders in the 1950s. During the Cultural Revolution it was enlarged again to include part of Inner Mongolia, giving it a border with Mongolia, but this was later reversed. The name comes from the Manchu phrase girin ula, meaning along the river, written in Chinese as jilin wula and shortened to Jilin.

Jilin is one of the three provinces of Northeast China, bordering North Korea and Russia to the east and south and Heilongjiang, Liaoning and Inner Mongolia. Its capital and largest city is Changchun, 113 kilometres west of Jilin City. The Changbai Mountains in the south-east hold its highest peak, Paektu Mountain at 2,744 metres, and the Yalu and Tumen rivers form parts of the border with North Korea. Agriculture centres on rice, wheat, maize and sorghum, and the province is known for ginseng and deer antlers used in Chinese medicine.
jilin-city: Jilin City lies in central Jilin Province, in a hilly area on the Songhua River, which surrounds much of the city and gives it the nickname River City. Four mountains stand round it: North Mountain (Beishan) to the west, Long Tan Mountain to the east, Zhuque Mountain to the north and Turtle Mountain to the south. With the river they form a bagua in the Taiji pattern. Beishan is the best known of them and is home to several Buddhist temples. The climate is humid continental, with long, cold winters. The Songhua is the only river in the region that does not freeze in winter, and water vapour rising from it crystallises on willow branches as rime ice in January and February.

Jilin City is one of the oldest cities in Northeast China. Under the Yongle Emperor, the Ming sought to extend control throughout Manchuria, and river fleets built here sailed several times to make local chieftains swear allegiance. After the Manchu-led Qing dynasty was established, the territory of today's Primorsky Krai was placed under Jilin's administration. As the Russian Empire advanced east towards the Pacific coast, the Qing government ordered a naval shipbuilding factory set up here in 1661.

Jilin was officially established as a fort city in 1673, when the Deputy Lieutenant-General Anzhuhu was ordered to build a castle. In 1676 the Military Governor of Ninguta was transferred to Jilin because of its more convenient location and growing military importance, and the city then developed rapidly. Its nickname comes from a line of a poem written by the Kangxi Emperor on his visit in 1682. Jilin remained important in the 18th and 19th centuries as one of the few cities beyond the Willow Palisade, with Qiqihar, Ninguta and Mukden.

When Manchukuo made Xinjing, now Changchun, its capital, Jilin's importance fell. By 1940 Jilin had 173,624 people and Xinjing 544,202. Soviet forces captured Jilin during the August Storm operation. It was the provincial capital of Jilin Province from the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 until Changchun took that role in 1956.

Jilin City is a prefecture-level city and the only major city in China that shares its name with its province. It co-hosted the Asian Winter Games in 2007, and winter sports such as skiing and skating are popular. Among its sights is Wulajie Old City, a walled Qing town downstream on the Songhua. It was a collecting point for local products sent to the imperial court, and the Kangxi Emperor went there in 1682 to fish for sturgeon. A Meteorite Museum there displays the largest stony meteorite of a documented meteorite fall.
jim-crow-laws: The Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery was ratified on 18 December 1865. During Reconstruction, between 1865 and 1877, federal laws protected the civil rights of freedmen in the South. In the 1870s Democrats gradually regained power in Southern legislatures while paramilitary groups such as the Ku Klux Klan, the White League and the Red Shirts drove out Republican officeholders and lynched Black voters to suppress the Black vote.

The term Jim Crow probably derives from Jump Jim Crow, a minstrel dance performed in blackface by the white actor Thomas D. Rice, first staged in 1828. By the end of the nineteenth century the name meant the social separation of the races.

The laws were passed by white-dominated state legislatures to remove the gains that African Americans had made during Reconstruction. Beginning in the 1870s they mandated segregation in public facilities across the South, and companion laws excluded most African Americans from the vote. The Civil Rights Act of 1875 guaranteed equal treatment in public accommodations but had little effect, and an 1883 Supreme Court decision found it unconstitutional in some respects.

In Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 the Supreme Court upheld the doctrine of separate but equal facilities. In practice the facilities for African Americans were consistently inferior and underfunded, and sometimes did not exist. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, campaigned against the laws and the doctrine.

In Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka in 1954 the Supreme Court unanimously held public school segregation unconstitutional and overturned Plessy. In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, and the Montgomery bus boycott that followed lasted more than a year. Mass demonstrations organised by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, headed by Martin Luther King Jr., drew national attention on television.

Congress overcame Southern filibusters to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which overturned most remaining Jim Crow laws. Laws against interracial marriage were struck down in Loving v. Virginia in 1967. Historians count the laws among the causes of the Great Migration, in which African Americans left the rural South for cities in the Northeast, Midwest and West.
jimena-diaz: Jimena, whose name is also spelled Ximena, was born before July 1046. She was the daughter of Diego Fernández, Count of Oviedo, himself the son of Count Fernando Flaínez, and of his wife Cristina, and she was a sister of Fernando Díaz, Count of Asturias. She married Rodrigo Díaz between July 1074 and 12 May 1076.

It is unclear whether she lived with her husband in the Taifa of Zaragoza during his first exile, from 1080 to 1086, when he led the army of its rulers, or whether she went to Asturias in those years. A legal action from Tol dated 1083 suggests that she kept a presence there even while the two were apart. At the start of his second exile, in 1089, she was imprisoned with her children Cristina, Diego and María by order of Alfonso VI. Nothing more is known of her until the end of 1094.

Rodrigo Díaz conquered Valencia on 17 June 1094 and secured it by his victory at the Battle of Cuarte on 21 October, after which Jimena rejoined him and stayed with him until his death. The principality he had founded was an independent state, and she succeeded him as its ruler. Their son Diego had been killed in 1097, fighting under Alfonso VI. A deed of gift that she made to the Cathedral of Valencia in 1101 survives with her signature. When the king judged the city impossible to defend, he escorted her back to Castile.

In 1103 she signed a document at the Monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña selling a monastery she owned to two canons of Burgos. This does not show that she spent her old age in the abbey, as the monastery maintained until the 18th century in the hagiographic texts known as the Legend of Cardeña; it is more likely that she lived her last years in or near Burgos. She died between 29 August 1113 and 1116, probably in 1116.

Through her daughters her descendants entered several ruling houses. Cristina married Ramiro Sánchez of Monzón and was the mother of King García Ramírez of Navarre, and María married first a prince of Aragon and then Ramon Berenguer III, Count of Barcelona. Jimena and her husband were buried at San Pedro de Cardeña. After the tombs were ransacked during the Napoleonic Wars the remains were reburied in Burgos, and they now lie in Burgos Cathedral.
jimmy-carter: James Earl Carter Jr. was born on 1 October 1924 in Plains, Georgia, at the Wise Sanitarium, where his mother worked as a registered nurse. He was the eldest child of Bessie Lillian Gordy and James Earl Carter Sr., a local businessman who ran a general store. The family settled in nearby Archery, a community populated almost entirely by impoverished Black families. His father was staunchly pro-segregation, yet allowed his son to befriend the children of the Black farmhands.

Carter graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1946 and joined the submarine service. In 1952 he began an association with the Navy's nuclear submarine program, led by Captain Hyman G. Rickover, who he later said had the most influence on his life after his parents. He then returned to Plains and expanded the family peanut-growing business.

Carter won a seat in the Georgia State Senate in 1962, after a repeat election because early counting was shown to be the result of fraudulent voting. He served from 1963 to 1967. Sworn in as the 76th governor of Georgia on 12 January 1971, he declared in his inaugural speech that the time for racial discrimination was over, which caused many segregationists who had supported him to feel betrayed. He merged about 300 state agencies into 22.

He announced his presidential campaign on 12 December 1974. Little known outside his home state, he was derided with the question Jimmy Who?. With the Watergate scandal fresh in voters' minds, his position as an outsider helped him, and he narrowly defeated the Republican incumbent Gerald Ford.

Inaugurated on 20 January 1977, Carter issued an unconditional amnesty for Vietnam War draft evaders. His administration negotiated the Camp David Accords, the Panama Canal Treaties and the second Strategic Arms Limitation Talks agreement, established diplomatic relations with China, and created the Departments of Energy and Education. His term was marked by inflation and recession, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran hostage crisis. He lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan in a landslide.

After the presidency Carter established the Carter Center to promote human rights, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002. He travelled widely to conduct peace negotiations, monitor elections and combat neglected tropical diseases, and he was a key figure in Habitat for Humanity. He died at his home in Plains on 29 December 2024, aged 100, and was buried next to his wife Rosalynn. Historians have generally rated his presidency below average, while his post-presidency, the longest in U.S. history, is viewed more favourably.
jin-song-wars: The two powers began as allies. After Wanyan Aguda united the Jurchen tribes and in 1115 named himself emperor of the Jin, the Song emperor Huizong sought his help against the Khitan-led Liao dynasty, hoping to recover the Sixteen Prefectures lost in 938. The Jin took the Liao capitals quickly, while Song attacks on Yanjing failed twice in 1122. By the treaty of 1123 the Song received only seven prefectures and agreed to pay the Jin 300,000 bolts of silk and 200,000 taels of silver a year.

The alliance soon broke down. Zhang Jue, a former Liao governor, turned his city over to the Song, though the treaty forbade harbouring defectors, and in 1124 Song officials asked for nine more prefectures. In November 1125 the Jin emperor Taizong ordered the attack.

Two Jin armies invaded. Kaifeng was first besieged on 31 January 1126, and after 33 days the new emperor Qinzong bought a withdrawal by ceding three prefectures; when he went back on the agreement the Jin returned and broke into the city on 9 January 1127. The Jin then tried to rule the north through puppet states, Da Chu in 1127 and Da Qi from 1130 to 1137. Gaozong, enthroned on 12 June 1127, was pursued as far as the sea in 1130, but the Song navy on the Yangtze and an insurgency in the north checked the invaders.

The peace of 1142 was broken twice. The Jin emperor Wanyan Liang invaded in 1161, was defeated at the Battle of Caishi in November and was assassinated by his own officers in December. Under the Song chancellor Han Tuozhou war was declared on 14 June 1206; the offensive failed, and the treaty of 2 November 1208 raised the tribute. Pressed by the Mongols, the Jin attacked the Song again from 1217 until a peace in 1224 ended the tribute. In 1233 the Song allied with the Mongols, and in 1234 their troops took Caizhou, where the Jin emperor Aizong killed himself.

Some two to three million Jurchens came to rule about 30 million Han Chinese in the north. Over half a million people fled south in 1126–1127. Lin'an, declared the capital in 1138, grew into a major commercial centre. The wars also spurred gunpowder weapons: the fire lance is first reported at the siege of De'an in 1132, and the iron-cased bombs the Jin used at Qizhou in 1221 are the first known hard-casing bombs. After the Jin fell the Mongols turned on the Song, which collapsed in 1279.
jingdezhen: Jingdezhen lies in the north-east of Jiangxi province, on the Poyang Lake Plain, bordering Anhui. It looks an unpromising place for potteries, a remote town in hilly country, but it stands close to the best deposits of petuntse, or pottery stone, in China and is surrounded by forests, mostly of pine, that fed the kilns. The Chang River carried fragile wares down to Poyang Lake and on to the Yangtze, from where they could reach the coast for export.

Kaolin, which the local kilns first used together with petuntse to make hard-paste porcelain, takes its name from the French Jesuit d'Entrecolles's rendering of the local term gaolingtu, from Gaoling, a village in Fuliang County that supplied most of the kaolin in the early and mid-Qing dynasty.

The area belonged to the state of Chu, then to the Qin and Han empires. The town was renamed Fuliang in 742 CE and Jingdezhen in 1004. In the Ming and Qing dynasties it counted as one of China's four great towns for commerce and industry, with Foshan, Hankou and Zhuxian. From the Ming period official kilns there were controlled by the emperor and made imperial porcelain in large quantity for the court and for imperial gifts; the imperial kilns stood in the centre of the town at Zhushan (Pearl Hill), with many other kilns four kilometres away at Hutian.

Its best-known wares were successively Qingbai ware in the Song and Yuan dynasties, blue and white porcelain from the 1330s, and famille rose and other famille colours under the Qing. It made a great variety of pottery for the Chinese market and for export. In 1855, during the Taiping Rebellion, Taiping forces destroyed all 9,000 kilns, which were rebuilt after the war in 1866. During the Cultural Revolution the town produced many porcelain Mao badges and statues of a seated Mao Zedong.

Jingdezhen is a prefecture-level city that kept the word zhen, town, in its name after it was upgraded in 1949, to honour its history. It was named one of China's historical and cultural cities in 1982. In 2004 it marked 1,000 years as an imperial kiln centre and as Jingdezhen. It still makes tablewares in great quantity and costlier decorative pieces, and its Ceramic Institute teaches the craft. A blue and white jar of the Yuan dynasty sold in London in 2005 for $27.7 million.
jingle-bells: It is not known where or when James Lord Pierpont first composed the song that became Jingle Bells. A plaque at 19 High Street in Medford Square, Massachusetts, claims that Pierpont wrote it there in 1850, at what was then the Simpson Tavern. The researcher Kyna Hamill proposes instead that he composed it in Boston, before moving to Savannah in the autumn of 1857.

By the time of its release Pierpont was organist and music director of the Unitarian church in Savannah, Georgia, where his brother Rev. John Pierpont Jr. was minister. In August 1857 he married Eliza Jane Purse, daughter of the mayor of Savannah, and he never returned north. The song belonged to the then-popular genre of sleighing songs, and Hamill argues that its lyrics closely resemble lines from many others and that Pierpont's need for money led him to release it as a financial enterprise. It was possibly intended as a drinking song and had no original connection with Christmas.

The song was republished in 1859 by Oliver Ditson and Company of Boston as Jingle Bells; or, The One Horse Open Sleigh. The music historian James Fuld notes that jingle in the title is apparently an imperative verb, though jingle bells is commonly read as a kind of bell. In pre-automobile New England horses' harnesses carried bells to avoid collisions at blind intersections, since a sleigh in snow makes almost no noise, and the rhythm of the tune seems to imitate a trotting horse.

The first two stanzas and the chorus of the 1857 lyrics differed slightly from the modern words, and it is unknown who changed them. The 1857 version also had a substantially different chorus. The simpler modern refrain has an unknown origin but dates back at least to 1898.

The song became associated with winter and Christmas in the 1860s and 1870s. The banjoist Will Lyle recorded it on an Edison cylinder on 30 October 1889, believed to be the first Christmas record, though no copy survives. The earliest surviving vocal recording, by the Edison Male Quartette, dates from 1898. In 1943 Bing Crosby and the Andrews Sisters sold over a million copies of their recording. On 16 December 1965 the Gemini 6 astronauts Tom Stafford and Wally Schirra broadcast it from space as a prank, with a smuggled harmonica and sleigh bells. The tune is also used for the French song Vive le vent and for several German songs, none with related lyrics.
jingzhou: Jingzhou is a prefecture-level city in southern Hubei province, on the banks of the Yangtze River. It covers 14,067 square kilometres on the Jianghan Plain, in the middle reaches of the river, and is crossed by a dense network of waterways and lakes. Wuhan, the provincial capital, lies downstream to the east, and Yichang, the Three Gorges and Chongqing lie to the west. The central urban area grew out of Shashi City and Jingzhou Town, which was also known as Jiangling. The city is named after the ancient province of the same name, one of the nine provinces of ancient China, which took its name from the nearby Jing Mountains.

The area has been inhabited for roughly 5,000 to 6,000 years, and the Daxi culture lived in present-day Jingzhou. Situated in the middle Yangtze, it has been a strategic military location since ancient times. The State of Chu was founded here, and Ying, an ancient city within the borders of present-day Jingzhou, became its capital in 689 BCE and remained so for over 400 years, through the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods of the Zhou dynasty.

In the Han dynasty and the Three Kingdoms era the area was known as Nanjun. Guan Yu lost the city to Eastern Wu in the Three Kingdoms period, which gave rise to the modern phrase dàyì shī Jīngzhōu, carelessness lost Jingzhou. Under the Tang dynasty it was the southern capital, Nandu. Jiangling was later the capital of the Southern Qi and Liang dynasties. In July 1949 the People's Liberation Army took the area, and in 1994 Jiangling County and Shashi City were merged into the city of Jingsha, which was renamed Jingzhou in 1996.

Numerous sites survive from the Chu period, including the ruins of five Chu cities, 73 sites with Chu culture and more than 800 ancient tombs, among them those of 18 Chu kings. Sites from the Three Kingdoms period include the Wulin Battlefield, where the Battle of Red Cliffs took place, and the Huarong Path. The city walls are 9 metres high and 10 metres thick, with a perimeter of 10.17 kilometres. The Jingzhou Museum displays a well-preserved male corpse about 2,000 years old, together with silk and lacquerware of the Warring States period.
jiuquan: Jiuquan occupies the westernmost part of Gansu, bordering Zhangye to the east, Qinghai to the south, Xinjiang to the west, and Inner Mongolia and Mongolia to the north. Its territory measures about 680 km from east to west and 550 km from north to south, and its built-up area lies mostly in Suzhou District, about 1,500 metres above sea level. The climate is a cold desert one, with long cold winters, hot and somewhat dry summers, and clear skies throughout the year. The legend behind its name tells that the young Han general Huo Qubing, after a victory over the Xiongnu, poured a vat of precious alcohol into a local creek to share its taste with his troops.

The place was founded in 111 BCE as Fulu, an outpost in the Hexi Corridor near the Yumen Pass on the overland Silk Road. It was a Han prefecture and under the Eastern Han an active military garrison. Under the Sui it became the seat of Su Prefecture and so took the name Suzhou; under the Tang the prefecture was renamed Jiuquan Commandery, and Jiuquan County was established in 624. In 763 the Tibetan Empire occupied it, after which it was controlled by the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, and in 1028 it was seized by Xixia.

In the Yuan dynasty Suzhou Lu was established under Gansu Province, and the city sometimes served as the provincial capital. It was a great centre of the rhubarb trade as well as a guardian of Silk Road traffic.

Under the Ming the Portuguese Jesuit missionary Bento de Góis was robbed at Suzhou and died there in 1607, during the journey that finally established that Cathay and China were one country. Meng Qiaofang took the city from Ding Guodong in 1649. The Hui under Ma Wenlu held it during the Dungan Revolt, and it was completely destroyed by the time the Qing general Zuo Zongtang recovered it in 1873, but it was swiftly rebuilt.

Jiuquan is a prefecture-level city of Gansu, served by China National Highway 312 and the Lanzhou-Xinjiang railway, and it is known within China as the first site of rhubarb cultivation. The Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, built in 1958, lies more than 100 km away, in the neighbouring Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. China's first crewed spaceflight, Shenzhou 5, was launched from it on 15 October 2003 with the astronaut Yang Liwei.
jizya: Jizya, from an Arabic word probably derived from the Middle Persian gazītak, a tax on the lower classes of Sasanian Persia, was levied on non-Muslim subjects of a state governed by Islamic law. The Muslim Arab conquerors largely kept the taxation systems of the Sasanian and Byzantine empires, and its origins are complex because the system arising from the conquests was not uniform but resulted from a variety of agreements. William Montgomery Watt traced it to a pre-Islamic practice in which a powerful Arabian tribe protected weaker neighbours for tribute, refunded if protection failed.

Jews and Christians in parts of Arabia began paying tribute called jizya during Muhammad's lifetime, at first as a share of produce and fixed goods rather than a poll tax. In the first century of expansion jizya and kharaj were each used for individual taxes, land taxes and collective tribute.

The Quran and the hadiths mention jizya without a limiting rate. Classical jurists understood it as payment for the protection the ruler gave, for exemption from military service and for permission to practise another faith with some communal autonomy. Most required it only of adult, free, sane, able-bodied men, and exempted women, children, the old, the sick, monks, slaves and non-Muslim foreigners staying temporarily; dhimmis who served in the army did not pay, and in some accounts the poor paid nothing. The rate was not fixed. Under Harun al-Rashid the jurist Abu Yusuf set amounts of 48 dirhams for the richest, 24 for those of moderate wealth and 12 for craftsmen and labourers, and payment could be made in kind.

The Bayt al-Mal, the public treasury, collected it, and in later times its revenues were commonly allocated to scholars. Jurists differed on its purpose: some saw a payment for protection, others an incentive to convert, and by the end of the 8th century some regarded it as a mark of inferior status.

In the Indian subcontinent Islamic rulers imposed jizya from the 11th century, and the Delhi Sultanate expanded it. After the Norman conquest of Sicily a poll tax on the Muslim minority, locally called gisia, continued the jizya of the earlier Muslim rulers of southern Italy.

In the Ottoman Empire jizya from Christian and Jewish communities was among the main sources of tax income; in Lebanon and Egypt it was paid by the community collectively as maqtu. In Persia the Zoroastrian minority paid it until 1884, when pressure from the Persian Zoroastrian Amelioration Fund led the Qajar government to remove it. It was eliminated in Algeria and Tunisia in the 19th century, with French colonisation, and continued in Morocco until the first decade of the 20th century. No Muslim state imposes it now.
joachim-murat: Joachim Murat was born on 25 March 1767 at La Bastide-Fortunière in Guyenne, in the present-day department of Lot, the youngest of six surviving children. His father, Pierre Murat-Jordy, was an affluent yeoman, innkeeper and postmaster who also served as steward for the Talleyrand family. His parents intended him for the church, and he studied at the College of Saint-Michel at Cahors and then at the Lazarist seminary in Toulouse. In February 1787 he left the seminary, either expelled or, as others say, having run away with a girl, and enlisted in a cavalry regiment, the Chasseurs des Ardennes.

An ardent Republican, Murat served in the revolutionary army and, at the royalist rising of 13 Vendémiaire in October 1795, brought the cannons of the Camp des Sablons to the centre of Paris, which let General Napoleon Bonaparte save the National Convention. He went with Bonaparte to northern Italy in 1796, commanded the cavalry in Egypt, where he led the charge that broke the Ottoman line at Abukir on 25 July 1799, and played a pivotal role in the coup of 18 Brumaire. He married Caroline Bonaparte in a civil ceremony on 20 January 1800.
Napoleon made him a Marshal of the Empire on 18 May 1804 and Admiral of the Empire in 1805. He fought at Ulm, Austerlitz, Jena and Eylau, where he led a massed cavalry charge against the Russians.

Murat was Grand Duke of Berg and Duke of Cleves from 15 March 1806 and King of Naples from 1 August 1808. In the Russian campaign of 1812 he was the best cavalry commander of the Grande Armée at Smolensk and Borodino, though he showed little concern for the horses, which starved and tired on the long marches. After the Battle of Leipzig he reached a secret agreement with the Allies to save his throne.

When Napoleon returned from exile, Murat changed sides again, and on 15 March 1815 Naples declared war on Austria. His army of about 45,000 invaded the Papal States and Tuscany, but he was defeated at Occhiobello and decisively at Tolentino on 2 and 3 May, and returned to Naples on 18 May. After Waterloo he fled to Corsica and tried to invade Calabria with about 200 men. He was captured, sentenced to death and shot at Pizzo Calabro on 13 October 1815. Murat and Caroline had four children.
joan-i-of-navarre: Joan was born on 14 January 1273 at Bar-sur-Seine in Champagne, the daughter of King Henry I of Navarre and Blanche of Artois. When her father died the following year she became Countess of Champagne and Queen of Navarre, and her mother Blanche acted as guardian and regent in Navarre. Foreign and Navarrese powers sought to exploit the heiress's minority and the supposed weakness of a female regent, so Blanche took Joan to the court of Philip III of France in 1274. By the Treaty of Orléans in 1275 Joan was betrothed to one of Philip's sons, and she grew up with the future Philip IV. It is uncertain whether she ever lived in Navarre as a child.

Joan married the future Philip IV on 16 August 1284, at the age of 11, and became queen consort of France a year later. Their three surviving sons all ruled as kings of France, and their daughter Isabella became queen consort of England. Philip is reported to have loved and respected her deeply, and in 1294 he named her regent of France in case his son succeeded him as a minor. She never visited Navarre, which French governors ruled in her name; they were unpopular, but loyalty to her was not questioned. She came no closer than Carcassonne in 1300.

In Champagne, a richer and more strategic county, she was an active ruler who visited regularly. In 1297 she raised and led an army against Count Henry III of Bar when he invaded Champagne, and she captured him and had him imprisoned while Philip took no part. She also brought a case against Bishop Guichard of Troyes, whom she accused of stealing funds from Champagne and from her mother by fraud. In 1305 she founded the College of Navarre in Paris.

Joan died in 1305, most likely from complications of childbirth. In 1308 Bishop Guichard of Troyes was arrested and accused of killing her by witchcraft, and he was released in 1313. She was buried at the Cordeliers Convent in Paris. Her eldest son became Louis I of Navarre in 1305 and king of France in 1314 as Louis X, and Philip V and Charles IV also ruled both kingdoms. Through her marriage Navarre and Champagne passed under the French crown.
joan-of-arc: Joan was born c. 1412 in Domrémy, a small village in the Meuse valley. Her date of birth is unknown. Her parents were Jacques d'Arc and Isabelle Romée, and her father was a peasant farmer with about 20 hectares of land, who also collected taxes and headed the local watch. Joan was not taught to read and write and dictated her letters.

She grew up during the Hundred Years' War, in a France divided between Armagnacs and Burgundians since the Duke of Burgundy had the Duke of Orléans assassinated in 1407. Domrémy's people were loyal to the Armagnac cause. After a raid in 1425 in which cattle were stolen, Joan had her first vision. She later testified that she saw Saint Michael, and later Saint Margaret and Saint Catherine, and that she swore a vow of virginity to these voices.

Joan met Charles VII at Chinon in late February or early March 1429, when she was seventeen and he was twenty-six. Theologians at Poitiers declared her a good Catholic, and women directed by Yolande of Aragon verified her virginity. Charles commissioned plate armor for her, and she designed her own banner.

She reached Orléans on 29 April 1429. At first a figurehead for morale with no formal command, she gained the support of the Armagnac troops and sometimes advised their commanders. On 4 May her arrival rallied soldiers retreating from the bastille of Saint-Loup, and they took it. After the victory at Patay, Charles was crowned at Reims with Joan at his side. The sieges of Paris in September and La Charité in November failed, and her role in these defeats reduced the court's faith in her.

Burgundian troops captured Joan on 23 May 1430, and she was handed to the English in November. Her trial for heresy opened at Rouen on 9 January 1431 under Bishop Pierre Cauchon. She was accused of wearing men's clothes, of acting on demonic visions and of refusing to submit to the church. The trial was politically motivated: her claims, if unchallenged, would undermine the English claim to the French throne. She was burned at the stake on 30 May 1431.

A court reinvestigated the trial in 1456 and overturned the verdict, declaring it tainted by deceit and procedural errors. Joan became a national symbol of France after the French Revolution. She was canonized in 1920 and, two years later, declared one of the patron saints of France.
joao-figueiredo: João Baptista de Oliveira Figueiredo was born in Rio de Janeiro on 15 January 1918, the third of six children of General Euclides Figueiredo. His father was exiled for trying to topple the Estado Novo regime of Getúlio Vargas in 1938, and two of his brothers also became generals. After studying at military schools in Porto Alegre and Realengo he was promoted to captain in 1944 and major in 1952. He was military attaché in Paraguay from 1955 to 1957 and became a general in the late 1960s. He headed the military staff of President Emílio Garrastazu Médici from 1969 to 1974 and then led the National Intelligence Service until 1978, when President Ernesto Geisel picked him as his successor.

The legislature, dominated by the pro-military National Renewal Alliance Party, elected Figueiredo easily against the nominal opposition candidate, General Monteiro. He continued the gradual abertura, or opening, begun in 1974. On 28 August 1979 he signed an amnesty law covering those convicted of political or related crimes between 1961 and 1978. The two-party system set up in 1966 could no longer be kept up, and the government dissolved ARENA and allowed new parties. In the general election of 1982 the pro-government Democratic Social Party won 43.22 per cent of the vote and the opposition Brazilian Democratic Movement Party 42.96 per cent, and the opposition won the governorships of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais.

Politics was overshadowed by economic crisis, with high international interest rates, the oil shock of 1979, soaring inflation and a foreign debt so large that Brazil sought help from the International Monetary Fund in 1982. In 1983 the Diretas Já movement demanded direct presidential elections, but Congress rejected the amendment. The opposition candidate Tancredo Neves succeeded him after an indirect election.

After the presidency Figueiredo did not return to politics and lived away from public attention in Rio de Janeiro. He died on 24 December 1999, aged 81, of kidney and heart failure, and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso declared three days of mourning. According to CIA documents he supported the continuation of summary executions of political dissidents. His presidency also saw several terrorist attacks attributed to hardline right-wing and military factions.
joao-goulart: João Belchior Marques Goulart, nicknamed Jango, was born on 1 March 1919 at Yguariaçá Farm in São Borja, Rio Grande do Sul. Most sources give 1918, because his father had a second birth certificate made adding a year so that he could attend law school. His father was a rancher who had been a National Guard colonel. Goulart graduated in law in 1939 but never fully practised; a knee paralysed by illness left him with a disability, and after his father's death in 1943 he inherited land that made him one of the region's most influential ranchers.

Encouraged by the former president Getúlio Vargas, a friend of his father, Goulart joined the Brazilian Labour Party (PTB) and later led it nationally. In 1953 Vargas appointed him minister of labor in a time of strikes. After Vargas's suicide he turned the PTB into a party of reformist character. He was vice-president under Kubitschek and, as president of the Senate, helped keep stability by negotiating with the trade unions, though conservatives accused him of promoting strikes.

As president, Goulart called for unity, democracy and reform. His first cabinet, led by the prime minister Tancredo Neves, was named on 8 September. A plebiscite in 1963 overwhelmingly rejected the parliamentary system and restored full presidential powers. His Basic Reforms plan proposed education reform using Paulo Freire's method, tax measures on multinational profits, votes for illiterates and low-ranking military officers, and the redistribution of unproductive properties over 600 hectares. Eletrobrás was created in 1962. Accused of communism, he denied it, and in 1967 even his accuser Carlos Lacerda acknowledged he was not a man from the Communist Party.

On 31 March 1964 General Olímpio Mourão Filho moved troops from Juiz de Fora towards Rio de Janeiro. Goulart went to Brasília, found no political support, and flew to Porto Alegre; Senate president Auro de Moura Andrade declared the presidency vacant, and Pascoal Ranieri Mazzilli was sworn in on 2 April. Goulart sought asylum in Uruguay on 4 April, farmed cattle, joined the Frente Ampla in 1966 and later lived in Argentina. He died on 6 December 1976 in Mercedes, Corrientes, apparently of a heart attack, though without an autopsy the cause is unconfirmed. About 30,000 people attended his funeral.
jodhpur: Jodhpur lies in the Thar Desert near the geographic centre of Rajasthan, about 250 kilometres from the border with Pakistan. Its name combines that of its founder, Rao Jodha, with the Sanskrit suffix pur, meaning city or settlement. The old city circles Mehrangarh Fort and is bounded by a wall with several gates. It is also called the Blue City for the dominant colour of the buildings in the old town. Average rainfall is around 362 millimetres but varies greatly: the famine year of 1899 brought only 24 millimetres and the flood year of 1917 as much as 1,178.

Marwar formed part of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire. A Rathore chieftain named Chunda received Mandore as a dowry from the Pratiharas and ruled there while the Tughlaq dynasty declined. Rao Jodha, a Rajput chief of the Rathore clan from Mandore, founded Jodhpur in 1459 after conquering the surrounding territory from the Delhi Sultanate. Mandore at first served as the capital but Jodhpur soon took over. The city stood on the road linking Delhi to Gujarat, which brought it a trade in opium, copper, silk, sandalwood and dates.

After Rao Chandrasen Rathore died in 1581, Akbar annexed the kingdom, and Marwar became a Mughal vassal with internal autonomy. Aurangzeb briefly took over the state around 1679 after the death of Maharaja Jaswant Singh, and Durgadas Rathore restored Jaswant's son Ajit Singh in 1707. Strife at court then invited the intervention of the Marathas. Under the British Raj Jodhpur was the largest state of Rajputana by area, and its Marwari merchants came to dominate trade across India. On 11 August 1947 Maharaja Hanwant Singh, the last ruler, signed the Instrument of Accession to India, having at first not wished to join. On 30 March 1949 the state became part of Rajasthan.

Jodhpur is the second-largest city of Rajasthan after Jaipur and the administrative headquarters of Jodhpur district and division, with about 1.6 million people. Its main sights are Mehrangarh Fort, Umaid Bhawan Palace, Jaswant Thada and the Ghanta Ghar clock tower, with Mandore Garden nearby. Local foods include Mirchi Bada and Mawa Kachori. It is a base for the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force, and a centre of the handicraft industry.
johann-caspar-lavater: Johann Kaspar Lavater, also spelled Caspar, was born in Zürich on 15 November 1741 and educated at the Gymnasium there, where J. J. Bodmer and J. J. Breitinger were among his teachers. At barely twenty-one he distinguished himself by denouncing, together with his friend the painter Henry Fuseli, an unjust magistrate, who was compelled to make restitution of his ill-gotten gains.

In 1769 he took holy orders in Zürich's Zwinglian Church and served until his death as deacon or pastor in churches of his native city. His oratory and evident conviction gave him wide personal influence. He was consulted extensively as a casuist and welcomed with enthusiasm on journeys through Germany, and his writings on mysticism were popular. In the same year he sent Moses Mendelssohn a translation of Charles Bonnet's Palingénésie philosophique and demanded that he either refute it publicly or convert. Mendelssohn refused both, and many prominent intellectuals, among them Lichtenberg and Herder, took his side.

Lavater became best known for his Physiognomische Fragmente zur Beförderung der Menschenkenntnis und Menschenliebe, published between 1775 and 1778. He introduced the idea that physiognomy related to the specific character traits of individuals rather than to general types. Its fame, which reached France and England as well as Germany, rested largely on the handsome style of publication and the accompanying illustrations. He drew chiefly on the writings of Giambattista della Porta and on Sir Thomas Browne's Religio Medici.

The work is credited with catalysing a golden age of silhouettes: Lavater held that the most accurate readings came from a traced profile outline, filled with black or cut from paper. As a poet he published Christliche Lieder (1776–1780) and two epics in the manner of Klopstock, Jesus Messias (1780) and Joseph von Arimathia (1794). From 1774 he was intimately acquainted with Goethe, who later quarrelled with him and accused him of superstition and hypocrisy. In 1788 William Blake annotated Lavater's Aphorisms on Man, which held 632 aphorisms.

In his later years Lavater's influence waned, and he drew considerable ridicule for his vanity. When the French took Zürich in 1799 he was shot by an infuriated grenadier while trying to appease the invaders. He died in Zürich on 2 January 1801, more than a year later. Ernst Gombrich characterised his influence as a physiognomic fallacy. The Swiss artist Warja Honegger-Lavater was his direct descendant.
johann-gottfried-herder: Johann Gottfried Herder was born on 25 August 1744 in Mohrungen, now Morąg in Poland, in the Kingdom of Prussia, the son of a teacher. He grew up in a poor household and educated himself from his father's Bible and songbook. In 1762, at seventeen, he enrolled at the University of Königsberg, where he studied under Immanuel Kant and became a protégé of the philosopher Johann Georg Hamann, who disputed the claims of pure secular reason.

In 1764 Herder went to Riga as a Lutheran pastor and teacher, and there he wrote his first major works, which were literary criticism. In September 1770 he met the young Goethe at Strasbourg, whom his criticism inspired to develop his own style, which can be seen as the beginning of the Sturm und Drang movement. In 1771 he became head pastor and court preacher at Bückeburg. By the mid-1770s Goethe, by then a well-known author, used his influence at the court of Weimar to secure Herder the post of General Superintendent, and Herder moved there in 1776, where his outlook shifted towards classicism.

Late in his career he endorsed the French Revolution, which earned him the enmity of many colleagues, and he and Goethe experienced a personal split. He was ennobled in 1802, and he died in Weimar in 1803, aged 59.

Herder was one of the first to argue that language shapes the patterns by which each linguistic community thinks and feels. In his Treatise on the Origin of Language of 1772 he defined language as the natural organ of the understanding. His most ambitious work, the four-volume Ideas for a Philosophy of the History of Mankind, was published between 1784 and 1791 and is regarded as an origin of the modern school of historical thought.

Germans had no nation-state until the nineteenth century, and Herder was among the first German intellectuals to base a national consciousness mainly on language and literature. He taught that every nation carries its own standard of perfection, and that the true spirit of a people lies in its folk songs, poetry and dances. He collected folk songs, published in 1773 as Voices of the Peoples in Their Songs, which Achim von Arnim and Clemens von Brentano later drew on for The Boy's Magic Horn. He refused a rigid racial theory, writing that there is only one species of man throughout the whole earth.
johann-gottlieb-fichte: Fichte was born on 19 May 1762 in Rammenau and baptized a Lutheran, into a pious family that had lived in the region for generations. He was the son of a ribbon weaver, Christian Fichte, who married Maria Dorothea Schurich somewhat above his class. Fichte attended the foundation school at Pforta from October 1774. Miltitz's widow supported him until 1784, which let him study theology at Jena and Leipzig, but when she withdrew her help he had to leave without a degree and worked as a tutor for several families, and in Zürich met his future wife, Johanna Maria Rahn.

In the summer of 1790 Fichte began to study the works of Kant. After a disappointing interview with Kant at Königsberg on 4 July 1791 he wrote, in five weeks, the Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation. The first edition appeared without his name or preface and was believed to be a new work by Kant, until Kant cleared up the confusion and praised the author, and Fichte's reputation soared. He married Johanna on 22 October 1793. He was invited to the University of Jena and began lecturing in May 1794, expounding his system of transcendental idealism with success.

In 1798 he was accused of atheism over an essay in which he argued that the living moral order is itself God. He was dismissed in 1799 and, since every German state but Prussia had joined the outcry, went to Berlin, where he joined the circle of Friedrich and August Wilhelm Schlegel, Schleiermacher and Schelling. In 1807 and 1808 he delivered the Addresses to the German Nation, which attempted to define the German nation. In the new University of Berlin, founded in 1810, he was unanimously elected rector, but resigned in 1812 after friction. He died of typhus on 29 January 1814, aged 51.

Fichte rejected Kant's things in themselves, the supra-sensible reality beyond perception, as an invitation to skepticism. He argued instead that consciousness is not grounded in anything outside itself and that the phenomenal world arises from consciousness, the activity of the I, and moral awareness. In Foundations of Natural Right (1797) he argued that self-consciousness is a social phenomenon: an individual becomes aware of itself as free only when other rational subjects summon it, and mutual recognition is a condition for the individual I. He is also the originator of thesis, antithesis and synthesis, an idea often attributed to Hegel in error.
johann-heinrich-pestalozzi: Pestalozzi was born on 12 January 1746 in Zürich, the second of three children. His father, a surgeon and oculist, died when Pestalozzi was five, and the family was supported with the help of their maid, Barbara Schmid. On holidays he visited his grandfather, a clergyman in Höngg, where he learned of the poverty of country peasants.

He was educated to become a clergyman, but the failure of his first sermon and the influence of Rousseau led him towards law and politics. At 19 he joined the Helvetic Society, founded by his former teacher Johann Jakob Bodmer. He exposed cases of official corruption and was held under arrest for three days; this made him many political enemies and ended his hopes of a legal career. He then became a farmer, married Anna Schulthess in 1769 and built a house called Neuhof on heavily mortgaged land that proved unsuitable for farming.

He published the four volumes of Leonard and Gertrude between 1781 and 1787, drawing on his knowledge of peasant life. In it a mother, Gertrude, teaches her children to live morally, and a schoolteacher, a clergyman and a politician follow her example.

When serfdom was abolished in Switzerland in 1798 he decided to become an educator. After the French army invaded Stans in 1798, the Swiss government recruited him on 5 December to run a new orphanage there; the first orphans arrived on 14 January 1799, in a dreadful condition of body and mind. He then taught at Burgdorf from 1800 and opened the Educational Institute for the Children of the Middle Classes in its castle in October 1800.

The institute at Yverdon opened in July 1805 and attracted visitors and pupils from all over Europe, with governments sending educators to study there. Disunion grew among his colleagues, and a state commission in 1810 praised his ideas but not the institute's practices, ending hopes that Yverdon would become a state institution.

Pestalozzi returned to Neuhof and published his Swansong, which provoked bitter replies from Fellenberg and Niederer. He fell ill on 15 February 1827 and died in Brugg two days later. His methods were child-centred and based on individual differences, sense perception and the pupil's self-activity, and he held that human nature is essentially good. Friedrich Fröbel, the creator of the kindergarten, was his student, and Charles and Elizabeth Mayo founded the formal education of infant teachers in Britain after Charles lived with him at Yverdon from 1819 to 1822.
johann-sebastian-bach: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach on 21 March 1685 (Old Style; 31 March in the new), the eighth and youngest child of Johann Ambrosius Bach, a violinist and director of the town musicians, and Maria Elisabeth, née Lämmerhirt. The Bach family spanned four generations of musicians across Thuringia. Little is known of his early years, and his musical education is largely conjecture: he probably had early instruction from his father and sang with the local schoolboy choir. He studied theology, Latin and Greek at the Latin school, with poor attendance, perhaps because of a string of family deaths: his mother in May 1694 and his father in February 1695.

In 1703 Bach returned to Thuringia and worked as a musician for Protestant churches in Arnstadt and Mühlhausen. He also paid extended visits to the court at Weimar, where he expanded his organ repertory, and to the reformed court at Köthen, where he was mostly engaged with chamber music. By 1723 he was Thomaskantor in Leipzig, responsible for music in four Lutheran city churches and for the St. Thomas School. He decided to compose annual cycles of church cantatas, and wrote for the university's student ensemble, the Collegium Musicum.
