Later scholarship places his birth around 482. Tauresium is most commonly identified with the archaeological site of Gradište, near the village of Taor southeast of Skopje in North Macedonia, though scholars debate the birthplace. From his uncle Justin he inherited ongoing hostilities with the Sasanian Empire.

Justinian reigned from 527 to 565 and pursued a restoration of the empire, partly realised. In 532 he concluded an Eternal Peace with Khosrau I at a cost of 11,000 pounds of gold. His generals Belisarius and Narses then conquered the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa and the Ostrogothic Kingdom, restoring Italy, Sicily and Dalmatia. The emperor himself never took part in campaigns.

The quaestor Tribonian oversaw the rewriting of Roman law. The first draft of the Codex Justinianeus appeared on 7 April 529, followed by the Digesta in 533, the Institutiones, a textbook, and the Novellae, new laws issued in Greek. In January 532 the Nika riots united the rival chariot-racing factions against him; he considered flight but stayed, apparently at the urging of his wife Theodora, and Belisarius and Mundus suppressed the revolt, in which Procopius says 30,000 unarmed civilians were killed. The destruction allowed him to rebuild the Hagia Sophia, completed on 26 December 537. In the early 550s two monks smuggled silkworm eggs from Central Asia.

Justinian grew isolated in his last years, and in the 560s he showed clemency to conspirators and pardoned Belisarius. He died in his sleep on the night of 14 November 565 and was succeeded by his nephew Justin II. Procopius, the main source, praised his buildings in one work and portrayed him as cruel and corrupt in the Secret History. The Corpus Juris Civilis is still the basis of civil law in many modern states, and many Eastern Christians regard him as a saint.
justinian-ii: Justinian II was the eldest son of Emperor Constantine IV and Anastasia. His father appointed him heir sometime after October 682, when his uncles Heraclius and Tiberius were deposed, and in 685, at sixteen, he became sole emperor. He was the last emperor of the Heraclian dynasty. His epithet Rhinotmetos, "the Slit-Nosed", recalls his mutilation after his first deposition.

The eastern provinces were stable when he ascended the throne. He raised the tribute paid by the Umayyad caliphs, regained control of part of Cyprus and in 688 signed a treaty with Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan that made Cyprus neutral ground with its tax revenue split. In 687 he removed 12,000 Christian Mardaites from Lebanon. In 688 and 689 he defeated the Slavs of Macedonia and entered Thessalonica, and he resettled the subdued Slavs in Anatolia as a force of 30,000 men. Most of them defected to the Arabs at the Battle of Sebastopolis, where Justinian was comprehensively defeated.

In 692 he convened the Quinisext Council at Constantinople. It highlighted differences between Eastern and Western practice, such as the marriage of priests, and he ordered Pope Sergius I arrested, but the militias of Rome and Ravenna sided with the pope. He created the theme of Hellas and tried to protect peasant freeholders against the aristocracy, but his taxes were unpopular. In 695 a rising led by Leontius, the strategos of Hellas, deposed him and cut off his nose, and he was exiled to Cherson in the Crimea.

In exile he gathered supporters, escaped and was received by Busir, khagan of the Khazars, who gave him his sister as a bride, whom he renamed Theodora. He then secured an army of 15,000 Bulgar and Slav horsemen from Tervel of Bulgaria, in return for a Caesar's crown and his daughter Anastasia's hand. In spring 705 he entered Constantinople through an unused water conduit and regained the throne on 21 August. His rivals Leontius and Tiberius III were executed, and his second reign was marked by war with Bulgaria and the Caliphate and by cruel suppression of opposition.

Cherson revolted under the exiled general Bardanes, who was proclaimed emperor as Philippicus, and Justinian was arrested and executed in November 711. His six-year-old son and co-emperor Tiberius was killed, ending the line of Heraclius. His coinage introduced the image of Christ and revived the loros, and he joined the office of consul to that of emperor.
justus-von-liebig: Justus Liebig was born in Darmstadt in early May 1803, the son of a drysalter and hardware merchant who made paints and pigments. As a boy of 13 he lived through the year without a summer of 1816, a volcanic winter that destroyed crops and caused famine in Germany, an experience said to have shaped his later work. He studied at Bonn under Karl Wilhelm Gottlob Kastner and followed him to Erlangen. On 26 May 1824, aged 21 and recommended by Humboldt, he became professor extraordinarius at Giessen, and he received the full chair in chemistry on 7 December 1825.

The university Senate refused to host an institute for training pharmacists and manufacturers, so Liebig ran it privately from 1826. From 1825 to 1835 the laboratory occupied a guardroom of a disused barracks, about 38 square metres, where he could work with eight or nine students at a time. Students came from many German states, Britain and the United States, and the laboratory became a model for teaching practical chemistry.

In 1830 Liebig developed an apparatus, the Kaliapparat, for determining the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen content of organic substances, which made quantitative organic analysis routine. With Friedrich Wöhler he showed that the explosive silver fulminate and the harmless silver cyanate had the same composition, which led Berzelius to propose the idea of isomers, and in 1832 their work on the oil of bitter almonds supported the doctrine of compound radicals. He founded the Annalen der Chemie, which he edited from 1832.

His book Organic Chemistry in its Application to Agriculture and Physiology (1840) argued that chemistry could raise yields and lower costs, and attacked the humus theory of plant nutrition. He emphasised nitrogen and minerals as plant nutrients and popularised the law of the minimum. A formula for beef extract, published in 1847, led to Liebig's Extract of Meat Company at Fray Bentos in Uruguay, of which he became scientific director in 1865.

In 1852 Liebig accepted an appointment from King Maximilian II of Bavaria to the University of Munich and became the king's scientific adviser, and in 1858 perpetual president of the Royal Bavarian Academy of Sciences. He had received the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1840 and was made a Freiherr in 1845. He died in Munich in 1873 and is buried in the Alter Südfriedhof. The University of Giessen was renamed Justus-Liebig-Universität in 1946, and he is called the father of the fertilizer industry.
jutes: According to Bede, the Jutes were one of the three most powerful Germanic nations that came to Britain, along with the Angles and the Saxons. From them, he wrote, descended the people of Kent, of the Isle of Wight and those in the West Saxon province opposite the island. Historians have no consensus on their origins. Bede inferred a homeland on the Jutland peninsula, and one hypothesis holds that they left Jutland after a Danish invasion and moved to the Frisian coast. Analysis of grave goods, however, links east Kent, southern Hampshire and the Isle of Wight to northern Francia or Frisia more than to Jutland, and some sources seem to use the names Frisians and Jutes interchangeably.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, which historians regard as giving foundation legends, says that Hengist and Horsa came in 449 at Vortigern's invitation to help against the Picts and landed at Ebbsfleet; later settlers came from the Old Saxons, the Angles and the Jutes, who took Kent, the Isle of Wight and Hampshire. It names Wihtgar and Stuf as founders of the Isle of Wight and Port with his sons as founders of the Meonwara in southern Hampshire. Contemporary writing is scarce before the 7th century, and some archaeological findings challenge the Chronicle's early dates. The Jutes probably settled Kent first and spread from there.

In 676 King Æthelred of Mercia ravaged Kent and destroyed Rochester. In 681 Wulfhere of Mercia advanced into southern Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, which he gave to Æthelwealh of Sussex. In the 680s Cædwalla of Wessex conquered Sussex and the Jutish lands in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. Bede says he killed the island's king, Arwald, and tried to destroy its inhabitants and replace them with people from his own province, but that Jutes remained the majority there. The island was then permanently under West Saxon control and the Meonwara joined Wessex. Kent kept its independence.

Brooches and bracteates found in east Kent, the Isle of Wight and southern Hampshire show strong Frankish and North Sea influence from the mid-fifth to the late sixth century. Kent was culturally distinct east from west until the late 6th century, when west Kent adopted east Kent's material culture. The Frankish princess Bertha came to Kent around 580 to marry King Æthelberht, bringing a bishop, and Pope Gregory I sent Augustine in 597. The Isle of Wight was the last area of Anglo-Saxon England to be converted, in 686. The Jutes practised partible inheritance known as gavelkind, which was kept in Kent until its abolition in 1925.
jutland: The Jutland peninsula stretches from the Grenen spit in the north to the confluence of the Elbe and the Sude in the south-east, and it is bounded by the North Sea, the Skagerrak, the Kattegat and the Baltic Sea. Its land is flat, with comparatively steep hills in the east. West Jutland has open land, heaths, plains and peat bogs, while East Jutland is more fertile, with lakes and forests. As a cultural region, Jutland usually means only the Danish part, though the Eider, which was the southern border of Denmark and the cultural and linguistic boundary between the Nordic countries and Germany from about 850 to the 18th century, is sometimes taken as its limit. The peninsula is also called the Cimbric peninsula.

According to Ptolemy, Jutland or the Cimbric Chersonese was the home of Teutons, Cimbri and Charudes. Angles, Saxons and Jutes migrated to Britain from around 450. The Angles gave their name to England, and the kingdom of Kent is associated with Jutish origins, as Bede says and the archaeology of Kent supports. From the 5th century the pagan Danes began the Danevirke, a defensive wall inland from near present-day Schleswig, to protect themselves from invasion by the Frankish emperors.

The pagan Saxons inhabited the southernmost part of the peninsula until the Saxon Wars of 772 to 804, when Charlemagne subdued them and forced them to convert. The Abodrites, Wendish Slavs who had pledged allegiance to Charlemagne, were moved in to settle the area, which was later called Holstein. In medieval times the Law Code of Jutland, the Jyske Lov, governed the part north of the Eider, as well as Funen and Fehmarn.

The peninsula is divided among three Danish regions and the German states of Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg north of the Elbe and a small part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. The Kiel Canal crosses the south of the peninsula so that ships need not sail around it. Until industrialisation in the 19th century most people lived as farmers and fishers; the farmers of West Jutland were mostly free owners of their land, which was never feudalised. Jutlandic dialects differ substantially from standard Danish. The Battle of Jutland of 1916 was fought in the North Sea to the west of the peninsula.
juvenal-habyarimana: Juvénal Habyarimana was born on 8 March 1937 at Gisenyi, in Ruanda-Urundi, into a wealthy Hutu family. He studied at the College of Saint Paul in Bukavu in the Belgian Congo and in 1958 began medical studies at Lovanium University in Léopoldville. After the Rwandan Revolution began he left and entered the officer training school in Kigali, graduating with distinction in 1961. He married Agathe Kanziga in 1962. In June 1963 he became head of the Garde Nationale Rwandaise, and two years later he was made Minister of the National Guard and Police. He served in several security posts under President Grégoire Kayibanda, including minister of defence.

On 5 July 1973 Habyarimana, then army chief of staff and minister of defence, seized power in a coup against Kayibanda. In 1975 he created the Mouvement Révolutionnaire National pour le Développement as the only legal party. Government remained almost wholly in military hands until a new constitution was approved in 1978, when he was elected president as the only candidate. He was reelected in 1983 and 1988, again unopposed, with 98.99, 99.97 and 99.98 percent of the vote. Every citizen became a party member at birth, and the people took part in compulsory weekly labour called umuganda.

At first he won favour among Hutu and Tutsi alike, but he came to follow the policies of Kayibanda, and quotas again disadvantaged Tutsi in jobs and universities. His support shrank to the akazu, a circle of Hutu from the north-western provinces of Gisenyi and Ruhengeri. Under pressure from France, the IMF and the World Bank and from his own citizens, he allowed other parties in 1990. In October 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front, a force of Tutsi refugees who had served in the Ugandan army, invaded from Uganda. France sent troops to help him, and the war went on for three years until the Arusha Accords of 4 August 1993.

On 6 April 1994 his private jet was shot down near Kigali International Airport. President Cyprien Ntaryamira of Burundi, the Rwandan army's chief of staff and others died with him, and the plane crashed in the grounds of the presidential residence. The circumstances remain unclear. Hutu Power media blamed the Rwandan Patriotic Front, while the Front and others accused extremists in his own party of planning it to provoke anti-Tutsi anger and take power.

His death set off a genocide against the Tutsi and against Hutu who had opposed the government or backed the peace accords. Within 100 days between 491,000 and 800,000 Rwandans were killed. His family fled to France. His remains were kept by President Mobutu Sese Seko of Zaire in a private mausoleum at Gbadolite, and on 16 May 1997 they were burned at Kinshasa.
